questions.stem: Sort these properties into sandy soil and clay soil.
questions.explanation: Big sand particles leave big gaps, so water runs through. Tiny clay particles are packed tightly, so clay holds water and becomes sticky.

questions.title: Soil and the Living Earth
questions.stem: Which are ways earthworms help the soil? Choose all that are right.
options: Their tunnels let air and water into the soil.
Their droppings, called worm casts, add nutrients.
They eat dead leaves and mix them into the soil.
They make the soil dry out.
They turn clay into sand.
questions.explanation: Earthworms tunnel, eat and produce casts full of nutrients. They do not dry out the soil, and they cannot change one soil type into another.

questions.title: Soil and the Living Earth
questions.stem: Why do earthworms need moist soil?
options: They have lungs that must stay wet.
They breathe through their damp skin.
Their eggs hatch only in puddles.
They eat only wet soil.
questions.explanation: Earthworms have no lungs. Oxygen goes in through their damp skin, so if the soil dries out their skin dries and they die.

questions.title: Soil and the Living Earth
questions.stem: Very sandy soil holds on to water and nutrients well.
questions.explanation: Sand has large gaps, so water drains through fast and takes nutrients with it. Adding compost helps sandy soil hold water and nutrients.

questions.title: Soil and the Living Earth
questions.stem: Why does water drain quickly through sandy soil but slowly through clay?
questions.model_answer: Sand particles are large with big gaps between them, so water runs through. Clay particles are tiny and packed tightly, so water moves slowly and is held.
questions.explanation: The size of the particles decides the size of the gaps. Big gaps let water through quickly, and tiny gaps slow the water down.

questions.title: Soil and the Living Earth
questions.stem: Use this key. 1. Is the soil gritty? Yes: go to 2. No: go to 3. 2. Does it fizz with vinegar? Yes: chalky soil. No: sandy soil. 3. Is it sticky and shiny when wet? Yes: clay soil. No: go to 4. 4. Is it dark with lots of rotting leaves? Yes: woodland soil. No: garden topsoil. A sample is not gritty, not sticky, and dark and crumbly with only a few leaves. Which soil is it?
options: garden topsoil
clay soil
woodland soil
sandy soil
questions.explanation: Not gritty takes you to 3. Not sticky takes you to 4. There are few leaves, so the answer is garden topsoil, a mixture of sand, clay and humus.

questions.title: Soil and the Living Earth
questions.stem: Plants grow best in soil that is ___ and has plenty of ___.
questions.explanation: Roots need water, air and nutrients (minerals). Moist, nutrient-rich soil gives plants all three.

questions.title: Soil and the Living Earth
questions.stem: Chalky soil fizzes when vinegar is added to it.
questions.explanation: Chalky soil contains chalk, which reacts with vinegar and makes bubbles. Sandy soil does not fizz.

questions.title: Soil and the Living Earth
questions.stem: Look at the layers of soil. Which number is the solid rock at the bottom?
questions.image_alt: Layers of soil numbered from the top: leaf litter, topsoil, subsoil and bedrock.
questions.explanation: Layer 4 is the bedrock, the solid rock under all the soil. Layer 1 is leaf litter (humus), 2 is topsoil and 3 is subsoil.

questions.title: Soil and the Living Earth
questions.stem: Look at the layers of soil. What is the name of layer 3, just above the bedrock?
questions.image_alt: Layers of soil numbered from the top: leaf litter, topsoil, subsoil and bedrock.
options: humus
bedrock
subsoil
topsoil
questions.explanation: Layer 3 is subsoil. It has less humus than the topsoil above it. Most roots and earthworms live in the topsoil.

questions.title: Soil and the Living Earth
questions.stem: Which animal tunnels through soil and leaves droppings that add nutrients?
questions.explanation: Earthworms tunnel through the soil. Their tunnels let in air and water, and their droppings (worm casts) are full of nutrients.

questions.title: Soil and the Living Earth
questions.stem: Match each picture to its part in soil.
pairs: tiny pieces of rock: sand, silt and clay
living things that mix and enrich the soil
questions.explanation: Soil is a mixture of rock particles, humus, water, air and living things such as earthworms.

questions.title: Soil and the Living Earth
questions.stem: Rina wants to improve her sandy soil. Which of these will rot into humus and add nutrients?
questions.explanation: Leaves are plant waste that decomposers can rot into humus. Plastic, bricks and coins do not rot and add no nutrients.

questions.title: Soil and the Living Earth
questions.stem: Rina's vegetable garden has very sandy soil. The plants dry out quickly and grow poorly. What should she add?
options: more sand to let the water through
stones to make the soil heavier
compost or manure to add nutrients and hold water
nothing, because sandy soil is always best
questions.explanation: Compost and manure add nutrients and humus, and humus holds water. More sand would make the problem worse.

questions.title: Soil and the Living Earth
questions.stem: After heavy rain, Tuli sees many earthworms on the path. Which is the best explanation?
options: The worms want to dry themselves in the Sun.
The rain makes them grow bigger and climb up.
They are looking for leaves to eat on the path.
The soil gaps fill with water, so they come up for air.
questions.explanation: When the soil is soaked, water fills the gaps where air used to be. Earthworms breathe through their skin, so they come to the surface to get air.

questions.title: Soil and the Living Earth
questions.stem: Farmers near the Meghna river can often grow two or three rice crops a year. What helps most?
options: The soil there is made only of sand.
The soil there is chalky and fizzes.
Rivers drop fertile silt on the fields every year.
There are no earthworms to disturb the roots.
questions.explanation: Bangladesh is a huge river delta. Each year the rivers drop fine silt full of nutrients, so the soil stays fertile.

questions.title: Soil and the Living Earth
questions.stem: Class 5 will keep earthworms in a clear 'worm hotel' for one week. Which things will keep the worms healthy? Choose all that are right.
options: moist, loose soil with some dead leaves
air holes in the lid
a spot in hot, direct sunshine
dry, tightly packed soil
a cool, shaded place
returning the worms to the garden afterwards
questions.explanation: Worms need moist, loose soil, food, air and a cool, dark place, and they should go back to the garden afterwards. Heat and dry soil would kill them.

questions.title: Soil and the Living Earth
questions.stem: Sort these actions into ones that protect soil and ones that harm it.
items: planting grass and trees on a river bank
keeping the soil covered with plants
leaving bare soil to wash away in floods
using far too much chemical fertiliser
dumping plastic rubbish in the fields
questions.explanation: Roots and compost hold soil together and feed it. Bare soil washes away, too much chemical fertiliser harms soil life, and plastic does not rot.

questions.title: Soil and the Living Earth
questions.stem: Joy's uncle says earthworms in his field are pests and wants to get rid of them. What would you tell him? Give two reasons.
questions.model_answer: Earthworms help the soil. Their tunnels let air and water reach the roots, and their droppings add nutrients, so plants grow better.
questions.explanation: Earthworms are soil engineers. They let air and water in and add nutrients, so a field with worms is usually healthier than one without.

questions.title: Soil and the Living Earth
questions.stem: Class 5C poured 100 ml of water through 100 g of each soil. The water that dripped through in 5 minutes was: sand 80 ml, garden soil 55 ml, clay 20 ml. A cactus needs a soil that does not stay wet. Which soil suits it, and how much water did that soil hold?
options: clay, which held 80 ml
sand, which held 80 ml
clay, which held 20 ml
sand, which held 20 ml
questions.explanation: The water held is the water poured in minus the water that dripped through: sand 100 − 80 = 20 ml. Sand holds the least and drains fastest, so the cactus roots will not sit in water.

questions.title: Soil and the Living Earth
questions.stem: Fatema sells vermicompost for 15 taka per kilogram (example). One worm ring makes 40 kg every 2 months, so one ring earns ___ taka in 2 months. With 5 rings, she earns ___ taka in one year (6 lots of 2 months).
questions.explanation: 40 × 15 = 600 taka for one ring. Five rings earn 600 × 5 = 3000 taka in 2 months, and 3000 × 6 = 18 000 taka in a year.

questions.title: Soil and the Living Earth
questions.stem: A farmer tested two tomato plots (example results). Plot A, with chemical fertiliser only, gave 120 kg. Plot B, with half chemical fertiliser plus vermicompost, gave 135 kg. Which conclusion is best?
options: Vermicompost will always give 15 kg more tomatoes on any farm.
Plot B gave 15 kg more, but the test should be repeated before we are sure.
Chemical fertiliser stops tomatoes from growing at all.
Plot A did best because it had more chemical fertiliser.
questions.explanation: Plot B did give 15 kg more, but the plots may differ in water, sunlight or pests. One test is not enough, so it should be repeated on more plots and in more seasons.

questions.title: Soil and the Living Earth
questions.stem: Soil takes hundreds of years to form but can be washed away in one flood. Why should we protect it, and how?
questions.model_answer: We grow almost all our food in soil, and it forms so slowly that lost soil cannot quickly be replaced. We can protect it with plants, trees and compost.
questions.explanation: Soil is a thin, slowly formed layer that feeds us. Plant roots and compost hold it in place and keep it healthy.

questions.title: Soil and the Living Earth
questions.stem: Imran tests which soil holds the most water. He pours 100 ml of water onto 50 g of sand and 100 ml onto 200 g of clay, and times 5 minutes for each. What makes his test unfair?
options: The two soils have different masses (50 g and 200 g).
He measured the water in millilitres.
He poured the same amount of water onto each soil.
He used the same time for each soil.
questions.explanation: In a fair test only the soil type changes. The mass of soil, volume of water, time, funnel and filter paper must all stay the same.

questions.title: Soil and the Living Earth
questions.stem: Fatema makes vermicompost in a concrete ring. Put the steps in order.
sequence: Fill the ring with cow dung, vegetable peel and straw.
Add the earthworms and keep the mixture moist and shaded.
The worms eat the waste for about 6 to 8 weeks.
Collect the dark, rich vermicompost.
Spread it on the fields or sell it.
questions.explanation: The worms need food and moist, shaded conditions. After about 6 to 8 weeks they have turned the waste into nutrient-rich vermicompost.

questions.title: Earth's Changing Surface
questions.stem: Rain, ice, heat and plant roots slowly break rocks into smaller pieces. What is this called?
options: erosion
weathering
deposition
evaporation
questions.explanation: Breaking rock into smaller pieces is weathering. Erosion is when the broken pieces are carried away, and deposition is when they are dropped.

questions.title: Earth's Changing Surface
questions.stem: Match each key word to its meaning.
pairs: rock and soil carried away by water, wind or ice
sand and silt dropped in a new place
flat land built up where a river meets the sea
sea water pushed onto land by a cyclone
questions.explanation: Weathering breaks rock, erosion carries it, and deposition drops it. A delta is built by deposition, and a storm surge is a wall of sea water driven by a cyclone.

questions.title: Earth's Changing Surface
questions.stem: Weathering and erosion mean the same thing.
questions.explanation: Weathering breaks rock into pieces where it is. Erosion moves the pieces away. They usually happen one after the other, but they are different processes.

questions.title: Earth's Changing Surface
questions.stem: When water freezes in a crack in a rock, it ___ and splits the rock. This breaking-up is called ___.
questions.explanation: Water takes up more space as ice, so it pushes the crack wider. Over many winters the rock splits. This is weathering.

questions.title: Earth's Changing Surface
questions.stem: Which of these cause weathering of rock? Choose all that are right.
options: rain wearing the rock
water freezing and expanding in a crack
roots growing into a crack
a river dropping sand and silt
heat and cold making rock crack
questions.explanation: Rain, ice, plant roots, and heat and cold all break rock into pieces. A river dropping sand and silt is deposition, which builds land rather than breaking rock.

questions.title: Earth's Changing Surface
questions.stem: Put the steps in order to show how a delta forms.
sequence: Rain, ice and roots break rock into pieces on the hills.
Rivers carry the pieces downstream.
The river slows down where it meets the sea.
The river drops its sand and silt.
Over thousands of years the deposits build up into a delta.
questions.explanation: Weathering, erosion and then deposition build a delta. Bangladesh sits on the largest delta in the world, built by the Ganges, Brahmaputra and Meghna.

questions.title: Earth's Changing Surface
questions.stem: Sort the changes into slow changes and sudden changes.
questions.explanation: Weathering, delta building and valley carving take hundreds or thousands of years. Earthquakes, landslides and storm surges can change the land in minutes.

questions.title: Earth's Changing Surface
questions.stem: Rivers are the strongest force of erosion in Bangladesh.
questions.explanation: A fast river in flood can carry huge amounts of sand and silt and wash away its banks. Every year riverbank erosion destroys homes and farmland along the Jamuna and Padma.

questions.title: Earth's Changing Surface
questions.stem: Why are landslides more likely on hills where the trees have been cut down?
questions.model_answer: Tree roots hold the soil in place and leaves slow the rain. Without trees, heavy rain soaks and loosens the soil so it slides down.
questions.explanation: Roots bind the soil together and leaves slow the falling rain. Without them, the soil becomes loose and heavy with water, and it can slide down the slope.

questions.title: Earth's Changing Surface
questions.stem: Explain how a river can both destroy land and make new land.
questions.model_answer: Fast water erodes the banks and carries soil away. Where the river slows down, it deposits the sand and silt and builds new land such as chars and the delta.
questions.explanation: The same river does both jobs. It erodes where the water is fast, and it deposits sand and silt where the water slows down.

questions.title: Earth's Changing Surface
questions.stem: Scientists look for patterns. Which statement describes a pattern?
options: Rivers in Bangladesh flood most during the monsoon, from June to September.
A tree fell down in our garden yesterday.
It rained in Dhaka last Tuesday.
Rafi found a smooth stone by the river.
questions.explanation: A pattern is something that happens again and again. Floods come in the monsoon every year, so people can prepare. The other statements describe single events.

questions.title: Earth's Changing Surface
questions.stem: Tectonic plates move a few centimetres a year. If one plate moves 3 cm each year (example), it moves ___ cm in 100 years, which is ___ metres.
questions.explanation: 3 cm × 100 = 300 cm. There are 100 cm in 1 metre, so 300 cm is 3 metres. The plates move slowly, but sometimes they slip suddenly and cause an earthquake.

questions.title: Earth's Changing Surface
questions.stem: Look at the river diagram. Number 1 is ___, number 2 is ___ and number 3 is ___.
questions.image_alt: A river from the hills to the sea with processes numbered 1 to 4: rock breaking up on the hill, the river carrying rock and soil, a delta forming, and the sea.
questions.explanation: On the hill the rock breaks up (weathering). The river carries the pieces away (erosion). Where the river slows near the sea it drops them (deposition) and a delta forms.

questions.title: Earth's Changing Surface
questions.stem: Which number shows erosion, where the river carries rock and soil away?
questions.image_alt: A river from the hills to the sea with processes numbered 1 to 4: rock breaking up on the hill, the river carrying rock and soil, a delta forming, and the sea.
questions.explanation: Number 2 is erosion: the moving water carries the broken rock and soil downstream. Number 1 is weathering and number 3 is deposition.

questions.title: Earth's Changing Surface
questions.stem: Look at the cyclone from above. Which number shows the eye, where the sky is calm and clear?
questions.image_alt: A tropical cyclone seen from above: number 1 is the calm centre, 2 the ring of strongest winds and rain, 3 the spiral rain bands, 4 the winds spinning around the centre.
questions.explanation: The eye (1) is the calm centre. The strongest winds and rain are in the eye wall (2) around it, so people must stay in a shelter even when the eye passes over.

questions.title: Earth's Changing Surface
questions.stem: Which picture shows a sudden change caused by tectonic plates slipping?
questions.explanation: When tectonic plates suddenly slip, the ground shakes in an earthquake. Cyclones, floods and tornadoes are caused by weather, not by moving plates.

questions.title: Earth's Changing Surface
questions.stem: Match each picture to what it can do to the Earth's surface.
pairs: pushes a storm surge of sea water onto the coast
shakes the ground when plates slip
drops fertile silt but can destroy homes
ice in the cracks slowly splits the rocks
questions.explanation: Cyclones, earthquakes and floods change the land suddenly. Freezing water in cracks changes mountains slowly, by weathering.

questions.title: Earth's Changing Surface
questions.stem: Which letter shows a valley, the low land between hills that a river can carve out?
questions.image_alt: Six landforms lettered A to F: a mountain, a hill, a valley, a cave, a plain and an island.
options: A
B
C
D
questions.explanation: C is a valley. Over thousands of years a river erodes the land and makes its valley deeper.

questions.title: Earth's Changing Surface
questions.stem: When the monsoon flood goes down, Mina's grandfather says, 'The flood brings gold.' What does he mean?
options: Floods wash gold dust down from the hills.
Floods only wash away weeds.
Floods drop fertile silt that helps crops grow.
Floods make the farmland larger.
questions.explanation: The silt left by a flood is full of nutrients, so crops grow well afterwards. Floods can also destroy homes and crops, so they bring both good and harm.

questions.title: Earth's Changing Surface
questions.stem: The radio warns that a cyclone with a storm surge will hit the coast tonight. Moung's family lives in a house near the shore. What should they do?
options: Stay at home on the ground floor.
Go to the beach to watch the big waves.
Walk to the cyclone shelter now, before the storm arrives.
Wait until the water reaches the door.
questions.explanation: A storm surge can flood the coast fast and drown people. Leaving early for a raised cyclone shelter is the safest choice. Waiting or going to the beach is very dangerous.

questions.title: Earth's Changing Surface
questions.stem: The ground starts to shake while your class is inside school. Which actions are safe? Choose all that are right.
options: Drop down and take cover under a strong desk.
Hold on to the desk until the shaking stops.
Run to the lift to get out quickly.
Stand next to a big window to see outside.
Stay away from heavy shelves that could fall.
questions.explanation: Drop, cover and hold on protects you from falling objects. Lifts can get stuck, and windows and heavy shelves can break or fall.

questions.title: Earth's Changing Surface
questions.stem: The riverbank near Rafi's village is eaten away a little more every monsoon. Which action is most likely to slow the erosion?
options: Plant grass and trees along the bank.
Dig sand out of the bank.
Cut down the bank's trees for firewood.
Build new houses at the very edge.
questions.explanation: Roots hold the soil together and leaves slow the water. Taking away sand or trees, or adding weight at the edge, makes the bank weaker.

questions.title: Earth's Changing Surface
questions.stem: A flood has passed through a village in Sylhet. Sort its effects into helpful and harmful.
questions.explanation: Floods bring fertile silt and fish, but they also destroy homes and crops and can spread disease through dirty water.

questions.title: Earth's Changing Surface
questions.stem: Imran says that floods have only harmful effects on Bangladesh. Is Imran right?
questions.explanation: Floods destroy homes and crops, but they also drop fertile silt on the fields, fill ponds with fish and refill groundwater. Their effects are both helpful and harmful.

questions.title: Earth's Changing Surface
questions.stem: An example table shows the cyclones that formed in the Bay of Bengal over 20 years: Jan–Mar 1, Apr–May 12, Jun–Sep 4, Oct–Dec 19. Which two periods together had the most cyclones, and how many was that?
options: Jan–Mar and Jun–Sep, 5 cyclones
Jun–Sep and Oct–Dec, 23 cyclones
Apr–May and Jun–Sep, 16 cyclones
Apr–May and Oct–Dec, 31 cyclones
questions.explanation: 12 + 19 = 31 cyclones out of 36 in total. The pattern shows that coastal people should be most prepared in April–May and in October–December.

questions.title: Earth's Changing Surface
questions.stem: Class 5D poured 500 ml of water onto a bare soil tray and onto a grass tray, three times each. The bare tray lost 62 g, 58 g and 60 g of soil. The grass tray lost 9 g, 12 g and 9 g. On average, how many times more soil washed away from the bare tray?
options: 50 times
3 times
10 times
6 times
questions.explanation: The averages are (62 + 58 + 60) ÷ 3 = 60 g and (9 + 12 + 9) ÷ 3 = 10 g. 60 ÷ 10 = 6 times. The difference, 50 g, is not the same as 'how many times'.

questions.title: Earth's Changing Surface
questions.stem: Arif wants to test whether grass stops erosion. He tilts the bare soil tray at a steeper angle than the grass tray and pours 500 ml of water on each. Which change would make his test fair?
options: Use more water on the grass tray.
Tilt both trays at the same angle.
Use sand in one tray and clay in the other.
Pour water from a different height on each tray.
questions.explanation: In a fair test only one thing changes: here, whether there is grass. The slope, amount of water, height, soil and tray size must stay the same.

questions.title: Earth's Changing Surface
questions.stem: In the same year, one part of a river in Bangladesh gains a new char while another part loses land. Explain how this can happen.
questions.model_answer: Where the water is fast, for example on the outside of a bend, the river erodes the bank. Where the water slows, for example on the inside of a bend or near the sea, it deposits silt and builds new land.
questions.explanation: A river erodes where it flows fast and deposits where it flows slowly. So one river can take land in one place and make new land in another at the same time.

questions.title: Earth's Changing Surface
questions.stem: About 300 000 to 500 000 people died in the Bhola cyclone (1970), about 3400 in Cyclone Sidr (2007), and fewer than 30 in Bangladesh in Cyclone Amphan (2020), when over 2 million people moved to shelters. (Estimates from the Cyclone Preparedness Programme and UN reports.) Which is the best explanation for the fall?
options: Cyclones have become much weaker.
Fewer people live near the coast.
Warnings, volunteers and cyclone shelters help people reach safety.
Storm surges no longer happen.
questions.explanation: Since 1972 trained volunteers, radio warnings, satellite tracking and thousands of raised shelters have helped people move to safety. The other explanations are not supported by the facts.

questions.title: Earth's Changing Surface
questions.stem: In Class 5D's tray test, the bare tray lost 62, 58 and 60 g of soil and the grass tray lost 9, 12 and 9 g. Which conclusions are supported by the results? Choose all that are right.
options: Grass reduced the amount of soil washed away.
Every test on the grass tray lost less soil than every test on the bare tray.
Grass stopped erosion completely.
The three repeats for each tray gave similar results.
Roots are the only reason the soil stayed in place.
questions.explanation: The grass tray always lost far less soil (12 g or less against 58 g or more), and the repeats agreed. But some soil still washed away, and the test did not separate roots from leaves.

questions.title: Earth, Sun and Moon: Days, Years and Seasons
questions.stem: The Earth spins on its ___ once every ___ hours, causing day and night.
questions.explanation: The Earth spins on an imaginary line called its axis. One complete spin takes 24 hours. The side facing the Sun has day, and the side facing away has night.

questions.title: Earth, Sun and Moon: Days, Years and Seasons
questions.stem: Why does the Sun seem to move across the sky from east to west?
options: The Earth spins from west to east.
The Moon pushes the Sun across the sky.
The Sun orbits the Earth once a day.
The Earth orbits the Sun once a day.
questions.explanation: The Earth spins from west to east, so the Sun only appears to move from east to west. The Sun is not really circling the Earth, and the Earth takes a whole year to orbit the Sun.

questions.title: Earth, Sun and Moon: Days, Years and Seasons
questions.stem: The Moon makes its own light.
questions.explanation: The Moon only reflects sunlight. We can see it because sunlight bounces off its surface. The Sun is a star that makes its own light.

questions.title: Earth, Sun and Moon: Days, Years and Seasons
questions.stem: Match each word to its meaning.
pairs: one spin of the Earth on its axis
the path of one object around another
questions.explanation: A rotation takes 24 hours, and an orbit of the Earth around the Sun takes about 365¼ days. The extra quarter days give a leap year every four years.

questions.title: Earth, Sun and Moon: Days, Years and Seasons
questions.stem: Put these planets in order, starting with the closest to the Sun.
sequence: Mercury
Venus
Earth
Mars
Jupiter
questions.explanation: The order of all eight planets is Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune. 'My Very Easy Method Just Speeds Up Naming' can help you remember it.

questions.title: Earth, Sun and Moon: Days, Years and Seasons
questions.stem: Sort these into what is caused by the Earth's spin and what is caused by its orbit around the Sun.
items: the Sun appearing to rise in the east
a leap year every four years
the changing seasons through the year
questions.explanation: The spin takes 24 hours and explains the daily changes. The orbit takes about 365¼ days. The seasons come from the tilted axis as the Earth moves around its orbit.

questions.title: Earth, Sun and Moon: Days, Years and Seasons
questions.stem: Which statements about the Moon are right? Choose all that are right.
options: It reflects sunlight.
It orbits the Earth about once a month.
Its phases repeat about every 29½ days.
It makes its own light.
It is a star.
questions.explanation: The Moon reflects sunlight and takes about a month to orbit the Earth, so the pattern of phases repeats every 29½ days. It is not a star and has no light of its own.

questions.title: Earth, Sun and Moon: Days, Years and Seasons
questions.stem: Why does the Moon seem to change shape during the month?
questions.model_answer: The Moon orbits the Earth, so from Earth we see different amounts of its sunlit half as it moves around.
questions.explanation: Half of the Moon is always lit by the Sun. As the Moon orbits the Earth, we see more or less of that lit half, which gives the phases from new moon to full moon.

questions.title: Earth, Sun and Moon: Days, Years and Seasons
questions.stem: What causes the seasons?
options: The Earth moving closer to the Sun in summer.
The tilt of the Earth's axis as it orbits the Sun.
The Sun getting hotter and cooler.
The Moon blocking some of the sunlight.
questions.explanation: The Earth's axis is tilted by about 23.5°. As it orbits, each half is tilted towards the Sun for part of the year (summer) and away from it for part (winter).

questions.title: Earth, Sun and Moon: Days, Years and Seasons
questions.stem: When it is summer in Bangladesh, it is winter in Australia.
questions.explanation: When the northern half of the Earth is tilted towards the Sun, the southern half is tilted away. So the two halves have opposite seasons.

questions.title: Earth, Sun and Moon: Days, Years and Seasons
questions.stem: Look at the planets in order from the Sun. Number 3 is ___, number 4 is ___ and number 5 is ___.
questions.image_alt: The Sun and eight planets in order, numbered 1 to 8 (not to scale).
questions.explanation: The planets in order are 1 Mercury, 2 Venus, 3 Earth, 4 Mars, 5 Jupiter, 6 Saturn, 7 Uranus and 8 Neptune.

questions.title: Earth, Sun and Moon: Days, Years and Seasons
questions.stem: Look at the stick and its shadows. When is the shadow the shortest?
questions.image_alt: A stick and its shadow in the morning, at midday and in the evening as the Sun moves across the sky from east to west.
options: morning
evening
midday
they are all the same
questions.explanation: At midday the Sun is highest in the sky, so the shadow is shortest. In the morning and evening the Sun is low, so shadows are long.

questions.title: Earth, Sun and Moon: Days, Years and Seasons
questions.stem: Look at the picture. In the evening, which way does the long shadow point?
questions.image_alt: A stick and its shadow in the morning, at midday and in the evening as the Sun moves across the sky from east to west.
options: west
north
south
east
questions.explanation: In the evening the Sun is low in the west, so the shadow stretches the other way, towards the east. In the morning the shadow points west.

questions.title: Earth, Sun and Moon: Days, Years and Seasons
questions.stem: Look at the Earth's orbit. In which month is the northern half tilted away from the Sun, so it is winter in Bangladesh?
questions.image_alt: The tilted Earth at four places in its orbit around the Sun, labelled June, September, December and March.
options: June
September
December
March
questions.explanation: In December the northern half is tilted away from the Sun, so sunlight is spread out, days are short and it is winter. In June it is tilted towards the Sun and it is summer.

questions.title: Earth, Sun and Moon: Days, Years and Seasons
questions.stem: Which number shows the full moon?
questions.image_alt: Eight shapes of the Moon numbered 1 to 8, from new moon to full moon and back again.
questions.explanation: Number 5 is the full moon, when we see the whole lit half. Number 1 is the new moon, 3 is the first quarter and 7 is the last quarter.

questions.title: Earth, Sun and Moon: Days, Years and Seasons
questions.stem: Look at the eight Moon shapes. Match each number to its phase.
questions.image_alt: Eight shapes of the Moon numbered 1 to 8, from new moon to full moon and back again.
questions.explanation: The Moon goes from new moon (1) through first quarter (3) to full moon (5), then through last quarter (7) back to new moon. This takes about 29½ days.

questions.title: Earth, Sun and Moon: Days, Years and Seasons
questions.stem: At noon in Dhaka, Priya's cousin in New York is asleep because it is night there. Why is it night in New York?
options: New York faces away from the Sun as the Earth spins.
The Moon blocks the Sun over New York.
The Sun moves around the Earth and skips New York.
Clouds cover New York at that time.
questions.explanation: The Earth is a sphere, so the Sun can light only half of it at a time. When Dhaka faces the Sun, New York is on the other side, facing away.

questions.title: Earth, Sun and Moon: Days, Years and Seasons
questions.stem: In Bangladesh, farmers need tube-well water for Boro rice but not for Aman rice. Why?
options: Aman rice is grown in winter and needs no water.
Tube-well water is warmer than rain water.
Boro rice is grown in the monsoon and floods the field.
Boro rice grows in the dry winter, when there is little rain.
questions.explanation: Boro rice grows in the dry winter, so farmers pump water from tube-wells. Aman rice grows in the monsoon, when rain fills the fields.

questions.title: Earth, Sun and Moon: Days, Years and Seasons
questions.stem: Imran's class wants to measure how a stick's shadow changes during the school day. Which steps are part of a fair plan? Choose all that are right.
options: Use the same stick in the same place each time.
Measure the shadow at several times, such as 9 am, 11 am, 1 pm and 3 pm.
Use a different stick each time.
Measure the shadow length with a metre stick or ruler.
Measure the shadow only once, at 3 pm.
questions.explanation: Keep the stick and place the same, and measure often so that you can see the pattern. One measurement, or a different stick each time, cannot show how the shadow changes.

questions.title: Earth, Sun and Moon: Days, Years and Seasons
questions.stem: Mina flies from Dhaka's cool December weather to visit Sydney, Australia. What weather should she pack for?
options: cold winter weather
hot summer weather
a monsoon like Bangladesh's
weather with no seasons at all
questions.explanation: Sydney is south of the equator. In December the southern half of the Earth is tilted towards the Sun, so it is the middle of summer there.

questions.title: Earth, Sun and Moon: Days, Years and Seasons
questions.stem: A family in Chattogram sees a full moon tonight. About two weeks later, they will see a new moon.
questions.explanation: The Moon goes from one full moon to the next in about 29½ days. After about half of that, around two weeks, it is a new moon.

questions.title: Earth, Sun and Moon: Days, Years and Seasons
questions.stem: Rina is reading about places around the world. Sort these facts into places near the equator and places far in the north.
items: about 12 hours of daylight all year
the Sun never sets for about two months in summer
the Sun never rises for about two months in winter
the biggest changes in day length
questions.explanation: Near the equator the Sun's height and the day length hardly change. Near the poles the tilt causes huge changes, from the midnight Sun to the polar night.

questions.title: Earth, Sun and Moon: Days, Years and Seasons
questions.stem: In the simulation, the Moon goes around the Earth while the Earth goes around the Sun.

sim.task: Open Gravity and Orbits. Choose Sun, Earth and Moon. Turn on the path display, then press play and watch the Moon and the Earth move.

questions.explanation: The Moon orbits the Earth, and the Earth with its Moon orbits the Sun. Gravity keeps each of them on its path.

questions.title: Earth, Sun and Moon: Days, Years and Seasons
questions.stem: What happens to the Earth when gravity is turned off?

sim.task: Open Gravity and Orbits. Choose Sun and Earth and press play. Watch the Earth orbit the Sun. Then turn gravity off and watch what the Earth does.

options: It stops moving.
It keeps orbiting the Sun in the same path.
It falls straight into the Sun.
It moves off in a straight line.
questions.explanation: Gravity pulls the Earth towards the Sun and bends its path into an orbit. With no gravity, nothing bends the path, so the Earth moves off in a straight line.

questions.title: Earth, Sun and Moon: Days, Years and Seasons
questions.stem: About how long does the Earth take to go once around the Sun?

sim.task: Open Gravity and Orbits. Choose Sun and Earth, press play, and watch the clock while the Earth goes once around the Sun.

options: about 1 year
about 1 day
about 1 month
about 10 years
questions.explanation: One orbit of the Earth around the Sun takes about 365¼ days, which is one year. One spin of the Earth on its axis takes a day.

questions.title: Earth, Sun and Moon: Days, Years and Seasons
questions.stem: In Dhaka (approximate data), the longest day is in June with 13.6 hours of daylight and the shortest is in December with 10.7 hours. How much longer is the longest day than the shortest day?
options: 2.7 hours
2.9 hours
3.1 hours
24.3 hours
questions.explanation: 13.6 − 10.7 = 2.9 hours, almost 3 hours. Adding the two numbers (24.3) does not compare them. The tilted Earth causes this change through the year.

questions.title: Earth, Sun and Moon: Days, Years and Seasons
questions.stem: Hours of daylight in Dhaka (approximate data) from January to December: 10.9, 11.4, 12.0, 12.7, 13.3, 13.6, 13.4, 12.9, 12.2, 11.6, 11.0, 10.7. Which statements are supported by the data? Choose all that are right.
options: The longest day is in June.
The shortest day is in December.
Days get longer from January to June.
July has longer days than June.
Every month has more than 12 hours of daylight.
questions.explanation: June has 13.6 hours (the most) and December 10.7 hours (the least), and the values rise every month from January to June. July (13.4) is shorter than June, and January has only 10.9 hours.

questions.title: Earth, Sun and Moon: Days, Years and Seasons
questions.stem: In 1610 Galileo used a telescope and saw moons going around Jupiter. Why was this important evidence?
questions.model_answer: It showed that not everything orbits the Earth, because moons were orbiting Jupiter. This supported the idea that the Earth and the other planets orbit the Sun.
questions.explanation: If moons can orbit Jupiter, then not everything has to orbit the Earth. This was strong evidence for Copernicus's idea that the Earth and the planets go around the Sun.

questions.title: Earth, Sun and Moon: Days, Years and Seasons
questions.stem: In June the northern half of the Earth is tilted towards the Sun. Which description of that month is correct?
options: Tromsø in Norway has polar night, and Sydney in Australia has summer.
Tromsø in Norway has the midnight Sun, and Sydney in Australia has summer.
Tromsø in Norway has the midnight Sun, and Sydney in Australia has winter.
Tromsø in Norway has polar night, and Sydney in Australia has winter.
questions.explanation: Tromsø is far north, so in June it is tilted towards the Sun and has the midnight Sun. Sydney is in the southern half, tilted away from the Sun, so it has winter.

questions.title: Earth, Sun and Moon: Days, Years and Seasons
questions.stem: The Earth takes 365¼ days to orbit the Sun. In 8 years the extra quarter days add up to ___ whole days. In 100 years about ___ leap days are needed.
questions.explanation: Eight quarters make 2 whole days, so 4 years need 1 leap day. In 100 years that is about 100 ÷ 4 = 25 leap days.

questions.title: Resources and Sustainability
questions.stem: A renewable resource is one that…
options: took millions of years to form and cannot be replaced
is replaced by nature quickly, or never runs out
is made by people in factories and sold in shops
can only be used once by a single person
questions.explanation: Renewable resources such as sunlight, wind, trees and fish are replaced by nature in a short time, or never run out. Coal, oil and gas are non-renewable.

questions.title: Resources and Sustainability
questions.stem: Sort these resources into renewable and non-renewable.
questions.explanation: Sunlight and wind never run out, and bamboo and fish grow back. Coal, oil and gas take millions of years to form, and metals such as iron are used up from the rocks.

questions.title: Resources and Sustainability
questions.stem: Put these in order from the fastest to the slowest to regenerate.
sequence: a hilsa fish population (1–2 years)
bamboo (3–5 years)
a mahogany tree (20–50 years)
a few centimetres of soil (hundreds of years)
natural gas (millions of years)
questions.explanation: Living things regrow in years or decades. A few centimetres of soil take hundreds of years, and fossil fuels take millions of years, so they are called non-renewable.

questions.title: Resources and Sustainability
questions.stem: Match each 'R' to an example.
pairs: say no to a plastic straw
turn off the tap while brushing teeth
turn old paper into new paper
questions.explanation: Refuse and reduce stop waste before it starts. Reuse keeps things in use, recycling makes new products from old materials, and rotting turns food and plant waste into compost.

questions.title: Resources and Sustainability
questions.stem: Coal, oil and gas are called ___ fuels because they formed from ancient living things. Using resources without harming future generations is called ___ use.
questions.explanation: Fossil fuels formed over millions of years from ancient plants and animals. Sustainable use meets our needs today without stopping future people from meeting theirs.

questions.title: Resources and Sustainability
questions.stem: Bangladesh makes most of its electricity from natural gas, a non-renewable resource.
questions.explanation: Natural gas is a fossil fuel. The gas fields in Bangladesh are slowly running out, so millions of homes now use solar panels and more solar parks are being built.

questions.title: Resources and Sustainability
questions.stem: A renewable resource can never run out, however much of it we use.
questions.explanation: Only some, such as sunlight and wind, never run out. Trees and fish are renewable, but they can run out if we take them faster than they regenerate.

questions.title: Resources and Sustainability
questions.stem: Which of these harm the Earth's resources? Choose all that are right.
options: catching too many fish, including young ones
cutting down forests faster than they regrow
planting a new tree for each tree cut
dumping plastic into rivers
protecting young hilsa so they can grow
questions.explanation: Over-fishing, over-cutting and dumping plastic all damage resources. Planting trees and protecting young fish help the resources regenerate.

questions.title: Resources and Sustainability
questions.stem: Why is natural gas called non-renewable, even though it was made by nature?
questions.model_answer: It took millions of years to form from ancient living things, and we are using it much faster than it can form again.
questions.explanation: Natural gas forms very slowly, over millions of years. People use it up far faster than nature can make more, so once it is gone it is gone for us.

questions.title: Resources and Sustainability
questions.stem: Which phrase best describes sustainable use of resources?
options: using as much as we can while it is still cheap to buy
never using any natural resource at all
using only the resources that cost nothing
meeting our needs without harming future people
questions.explanation: Sustainable use means we can meet our needs today and people in the future can still meet theirs.

questions.title: Resources and Sustainability
questions.stem: Trees are renewable, yet some forests disappear. Which is the best explanation?
options: Renewable resources are never changed by anything people do.
Trees stop growing once they are about ten years old.
People cut trees faster than the forest can grow back.
Forests are made of non-renewable materials.
questions.explanation: A forest can take 20 to 50 years or more to regrow. If trees are cut faster than they grow back, the forest shrinks, so even renewable resources can run out.

questions.title: Resources and Sustainability
questions.stem: Planting a new tree for every tree that is cut down is a sustainable way to use a forest.
questions.explanation: The forest regrows about as fast as it is used, so there will still be trees for future generations. This is sustainable.

questions.title: Resources and Sustainability
questions.stem: Which picture shows an energy source that will never run out?
questions.explanation: Wind never runs out, so it is renewable. Cars and factories mostly burn fossil fuels, which take millions of years to form.

questions.title: Resources and Sustainability
questions.stem: Match each picture to the 'R' it shows.
pairs: reuse: use it again and again
recycle: make it into a new product
rot: compost food and plant waste
refuse: say no to what you do not need
questions.explanation: The 5 Rs are refuse, reduce, reuse, recycle and rot. Each one helps to save resources and cut down waste.

questions.title: Resources and Sustainability
questions.stem: Which picture shows a renewable resource that can still run out if people take too much?
questions.explanation: Fish are renewable because they breed, but if too many adults and young fish are caught, the numbers fall. Sunlight and wind cannot be used up.

questions.title: Resources and Sustainability
questions.stem: Dhaka banned thin plastic bags in 2002 because they blocked drains. Which picture shows a better choice for carrying shopping?
questions.explanation: A reusable bag can be used again and again, so it replaces many thin plastic bags. This is the 'reuse' and 'refuse' idea.

questions.title: Resources and Sustainability
questions.stem: Sort the pictures into actions that help the Earth and actions that harm it.
questions.explanation: Planting trees, recycling and using solar energy protect resources. Oil spills and smoke from burning fuels pollute the land, water and air.

questions.title: Resources and Sustainability
questions.stem: At a river market, a seller offers Nadia a basket of tiny jatka (young hilsa) cheaply. What is the best choice for the future of the hilsa?
options: Buy them, because small fish taste the sweetest.
Buy them, because the fish have already been caught anyway.
Do not buy them: they need time to grow and breed.
Buy them, because hilsa will always come back.
questions.explanation: Jatka are young fish that have not yet bred. Catching them is banned for several months so that they can grow up and lay eggs, which keeps the hilsa population renewable.

questions.title: Resources and Sustainability
questions.stem: Class 5A found that most of their week's rubbish was paper and food waste. Which plan would cut the most waste?
options: Ask everyone to bring more new paper each week.
Buy more plastic wrappers to keep the snacks fresh and clean.
Put the paper and the food waste in the same bin.
Use both sides of the paper and compost the food waste.
questions.explanation: Using both sides of paper is 'reduce', and composting food waste is 'rot'. Both turn waste into something useful or stop it being made.

questions.title: Resources and Sustainability
questions.stem: Tuli wants to save resources at home. Which actions would help? Choose all that are right.
options: Turn off fans and lights when leaving a room.
Fix a dripping tap.
Leave the tap running while brushing teeth.
Carry water in a reusable bottle.
Throw all food waste into the drain.
questions.explanation: Saving electricity, mending leaks and reusing a bottle all reduce waste. A running tap wastes water, and food waste in the drain blocks it, when it could be composted.

questions.title: Resources and Sustainability
questions.stem: The gas fields in Bangladesh are slowly running out. Which choice is best for the future?
options: Use up the remaining gas as fast as we possibly can.
Stop making any electricity in the country.
Build more solar parks and solar roofs.
Install diesel generators in every village and city.
questions.explanation: Sunlight is renewable and never runs out, so solar power can meet our needs now without taking away the needs of future generations. Gas and diesel are non-renewable.

questions.title: Resources and Sustainability
questions.stem: Banning thin plastic bags in 2002 helped Dhaka, because the bags had been blocking drains and making floods worse.
questions.explanation: Bangladesh was one of the first countries to ban thin plastic bags. Fewer bags in the drains means less flooding, and less plastic in rivers and soil harms fewer animals.

questions.title: Resources and Sustainability
questions.stem: What happens to the temperature when you add more greenhouse gases?

sim.task: Open Greenhouse Effect. Find the control for the amount of greenhouse gases. Make the amount bigger and watch the thermometer and the heat that goes back up from the Earth.

options: It goes up because more heat is trapped.
It goes down because more heat escapes.
It stays the same whatever the gases do.
It drops to zero straight away.
questions.explanation: Greenhouse gases trap heat that would otherwise escape, so the temperature rises. Burning fossil fuels such as coal, oil and gas adds greenhouse gases to the air.

questions.title: Resources and Sustainability
questions.stem: When you reduce the amount of greenhouse gases, less heat is trapped and the temperature goes down.

sim.task: Open Greenhouse Effect. Use the control for the amount of greenhouse gases to make the amount smaller. Watch the thermometer.

questions.explanation: With fewer greenhouse gases, more heat escapes back into space, so the temperature falls. Using less fuel is one way people can help.

questions.title: Resources and Sustainability
questions.stem: In one week Class 5A collected rubbish (in grams): paper and card 1800, plastic 950, food waste 1200, pencil shavings 150, other 300. The total is ___ g. Food waste and pencil shavings, which can be composted, make ___ g.
questions.explanation: 1800 + 950 + 1200 + 150 + 300 = 4400 g. Compostable waste is 1200 + 150 = 1350 g, so about three tenths of the rubbish could rot into compost.

questions.title: Resources and Sustainability
questions.stem: The hilsa catch in Bangladesh was about 3.0 lakh tonnes in 2008–09 and about 5.7 lakh tonnes in 2020–21 (1 lakh = 100 000). About how many more tonnes were caught in 2020–21?
options: 2.7 tonnes
27 000 tonnes
270 000 tonnes
2 700 000 tonnes
questions.explanation: 5.7 − 3.0 = 2.7 lakh tonnes, and 2.7 × 100 000 = 270 000 tonnes. The catch rose because the fishing bans let more fish breed and grow.

questions.title: Resources and Sustainability
questions.stem: Sumi says, 'Bamboo is renewable, so we can cut as much as we like.' What is wrong with her idea?
options: Bamboo is non-renewable, so it can never regrow.
It can still run out if we cut it faster than it regrows.
Bamboo takes millions of years to grow back again.
Nothing is wrong, since renewable always means unlimited.
questions.explanation: Bamboo regrows in 3 to 5 years, so it is renewable. But if we cut it faster than it regrows, we will run out. Renewable does not mean unlimited.

questions.title: Resources and Sustainability
questions.stem: Fishing for hilsa is banned for several months of the year and for 22 days in the main breeding season. Explain how this helps both the fish and the fishing families in the future.
questions.model_answer: The bans let adult hilsa breed and the young fish grow up, so the population grows back. Then fishers can keep catching fish in the future.
questions.explanation: Hilsa are renewable only if enough are left to breed. The bans give them time to regenerate, so the catch rises and families can keep fishing.

questions.title: Resources and Sustainability
questions.stem: A woodcutter cuts 10 mahogany trees each year (example). Each tree needs about 50 years to grow back. How many trees must the forest have so that this can go on for ever?
options: 500 trees
60 trees
100 trees
5 trees
questions.explanation: In 50 years the woodcutter cuts 10 × 50 = 500 trees. With 500 trees, the first trees cut have regrown by the time the last are cut, so the cutting is sustainable.

questions.title: Resources and Sustainability
questions.stem: Approximate hilsa catch in lakh tonnes: 2008–09: 3.0, 2012–13: 3.5, 2016–17: 5.0, 2020–21: 5.7. Which statements are supported by the data? Choose all that are right.
options: The catch rose in every period shown.
The catch almost doubled between 2008–09 and 2020–21.
The bans are the only possible cause of the rise.
The biggest rise was between 2012–13 and 2016–17.
The catch in 2016–17 was 50 000 tonnes.
questions.explanation: The rises were 0.5, 1.5 and 0.7 lakh tonnes, and 5.7 is almost twice 3.0. The data cannot show that bans are the only cause, and 5.0 lakh tonnes is 500 000 tonnes, not 50 000.

questions.title: States of Matter: Evaporation, Condensation, Boiling and Melting
questions.stem: Pure water boils at ___ °C and ice melts at ___ °C.
questions.explanation: Water boils at 100 °C. Ice melts at 0 °C, which is also the temperature at which water freezes.

questions.title: States of Matter: Evaporation, Condensation, Boiling and Melting
questions.stem: Evaporation can only happen when water is at 100 °C.
questions.explanation: Evaporation happens at the surface of a liquid at any temperature. Wet clothes dry on a cool day too, just more slowly. Boiling is the change that happens at 100 °C.

questions.title: States of Matter: Evaporation, Condensation, Boiling and Melting
questions.stem: Match each change of state to what happens.
questions.explanation: Melting and freezing are opposites, and so are evaporation and condensation. Heating causes melting and evaporation; cooling causes freezing and condensation.

questions.title: States of Matter: Evaporation, Condensation, Boiling and Melting
questions.stem: Match each state of matter to how its particles behave.
pairs: close together, sliding past each other
far apart, moving fast in all directions
questions.explanation: A solid keeps its shape because its particles cannot move away. A liquid flows because its particles slide past each other. A gas spreads out because its particles are far apart and move quickly.

questions.title: States of Matter: Evaporation, Condensation, Boiling and Melting
questions.stem: Each change needs heat to be added or heat to be removed. Sort them.
items: a puddle drying up in the sun
dew forming on grass at night
steam turning into drops on a cold lid
questions.explanation: Melting, evaporating and boiling happen when heat is added. Freezing and condensing happen when heat is taken away.

questions.title: States of Matter: Evaporation, Condensation, Boiling and Melting
questions.stem: A glass of cold lemon sherbet 'sweats' on a hot day. Put the steps in order.
sequence: Warm air containing invisible water vapour touches the cold glass.
The water vapour cools down.
The water vapour condenses into tiny drops of liquid water.
The drops gather on the outside of the glass.
questions.explanation: Air always holds some invisible water vapour. When the vapour meets a cold surface it cools and condenses. The water comes from the air, not from inside the glass.

questions.title: States of Matter: Evaporation, Condensation, Boiling and Melting
questions.stem: Which of these make water evaporate faster? Choose all that are right.
options: a warm, sunny day
a strong breeze
spreading the water out in a wide, thin layer
putting a lid over the water
moving the water into a cold fridge
questions.explanation: Evaporation is faster when it is warmer, windier and when the surface area is larger. A lid traps the vapour and a cold fridge is cooler, so both slow evaporation down.

questions.title: States of Matter: Evaporation, Condensation, Boiling and Melting
questions.stem: Which sentence about boiling water is correct?
options: Its temperature keeps rising above 100 °C.
It happens at any temperature.
It happens only at the surface.
Bubbles of water vapour form all through the liquid.
questions.explanation: In boiling, bubbles of water vapour form throughout the liquid, and the temperature stays at 100 °C. Changing only at the surface, at any temperature, describes evaporation.

questions.title: States of Matter: Evaporation, Condensation, Boiling and Melting
questions.stem: When salty water evaporates, the ___ is left behind because it does not ___.
questions.explanation: Only the water turns into a gas. The dissolved salt stays behind as crystals. This is how salt is made from sea water.

questions.title: States of Matter: Evaporation, Condensation, Boiling and Melting
questions.stem: Explain the difference between evaporation and boiling.
questions.model_answer: Evaporation happens only at the surface of a liquid and at any temperature. Boiling happens all through the liquid, with bubbles, at the boiling point (100 °C for water).
questions.explanation: Both change a liquid into a gas. Evaporation is slow and only from the surface at any temperature. Boiling is fast, with bubbles forming throughout the liquid, once the boiling point is reached.

questions.title: States of Matter: Evaporation, Condensation, Boiling and Melting
questions.stem: Look at the water cycle. Which number shows **evaporation**?
questions.image_alt: The water cycle with five stages numbered: 1 evaporation, 2 condensation, 3 precipitation, 4 collection, 5 transpiration.
questions.explanation: In evaporation (1), the Sun warms liquid water in the sea, rivers and lakes and it turns into water vapour. Condensation (2) is the reverse.

questions.title: States of Matter: Evaporation, Condensation, Boiling and Melting
questions.stem: Look at the water cycle. Which number shows water vapour cooling and changing into tiny drops to make clouds?
questions.image_alt: The water cycle with five stages numbered: 1 evaporation, 2 condensation, 3 precipitation, 4 collection, 5 transpiration.
questions.explanation: High in the air it is cold. Water vapour cools and condenses into tiny drops of liquid water, which form clouds. This is condensation (2).

questions.title: States of Matter: Evaporation, Condensation, Boiling and Melting
questions.stem: Chocolate melts at about 30–35 °C. Which thermometer shows a temperature at which chocolate would melt?
questions.image_alt: Three thermometers A, B and C reading 5 °C, 25 °C and 40 °C.
options: A
B
C
questions.explanation: Thermometer C reads 40 °C, which is above the melting point of chocolate. A (5 °C) and B (25 °C) are too cool, so the chocolate stays solid.

questions.title: States of Matter: Evaporation, Condensation, Boiling and Melting
questions.stem: Match each picture to the change of state it shows.

pairs.text: ice cream left in the sun

questions.explanation: Ice cream melts when heated. A kettle boils. Water freezes in the freezer. A wet shirt dries by evaporation. Drops on a cold drink are condensation from the air.

questions.title: States of Matter: Evaporation, Condensation, Boiling and Melting
questions.stem: Which of these is made when water vapour in the air cools and condenses?
questions.explanation: Fog is made of tiny drops of liquid water that form when water vapour in cool air condenses. Sunshine, wind and fire are not made this way.

questions.title: States of Matter: Evaporation, Condensation, Boiling and Melting
questions.stem: Look at the particle pictures and the arrows between them. Heat is taken away from the gas on the right. What happens first?
questions.image_alt: Three boxes of particles: solid on the left (packed in rows), liquid in the middle (touching, jumbled) and gas on the right (far apart). Arrows labelled melting, freezing, evaporating and condensing join them.
options: It condenses into a liquid in the middle.
It melts into a solid on the left.
It evaporates into a liquid in the middle.
It freezes into a solid on the left.
questions.explanation: Removing heat from a gas makes it condense into a liquid, shown by the arrow labelled condensing. The gas must pass through the liquid state before it could freeze.

questions.title: States of Matter: Evaporation, Condensation, Boiling and Melting
questions.stem: Mina's mother has washed the school uniforms. Where will they dry fastest?
options: Folded in a pile on a hot, windy day.
Spread out on a line on a hot, windy day.
Spread out on a line on a cool, damp day.
Folded in a bucket in a shady room.
questions.explanation: Warmth, wind and a large surface area all speed up evaporation. Spreading the uniforms out on a hot, windy day gives all three.

questions.title: States of Matter: Evaporation, Condensation, Boiling and Melting
questions.stem: Raju takes a cold bottle of water out of the fridge on a hot day. Soon the outside is covered with drops. Where did the drops come from?
options: Water vapour in the air touched the cold bottle and condensed.
Water leaked out through tiny holes in the bottle.
The cold bottle made new water out of the cold.
Water inside the bottle evaporated and stuck to the outside.
questions.explanation: The air around us always holds invisible water vapour. When it touches the cold bottle it cools and condenses into drops. The water does not come from inside the bottle.

questions.title: States of Matter: Evaporation, Condensation, Boiling and Melting
questions.stem: Many homes in Bangladesh keep drinking water in a clay pot (kolshi), and the water stays cool. How does the clay pot keep the water cool?
options: Clay makes cold, which flows into the water.
Water seeps to the outside and evaporates, taking heat from the pot.
Water vapour condenses on the inside of the pot.
The pot sends its heat down into the ground.
questions.explanation: A little water seeps through the clay and evaporates from the outer surface. Evaporation takes heat from the pot, so the water inside is cooled.

questions.title: States of Matter: Evaporation, Condensation, Boiling and Melting
questions.stem: Moung spreads wet paddy (rice grains) on a mat in the sun. Which actions will help it dry faster? Choose all that are right.
options: spread it in a thin layer
heap it into one big pile
turn it over now and then
cover it with a plastic sheet
put it in the sunniest spot
questions.explanation: A thin layer gives a large surface area, turning brings wet grains to the top, and sunshine adds heat, so the water evaporates faster. A pile or a cover traps the water vapour.

questions.title: States of Matter: Evaporation, Condensation, Boiling and Melting
questions.stem: Imran's mother lifts the lid from a pot of boiling rice. The steam is very hot, so she tilts the lid so that the opening faces away from her face and arms. This is the safe thing to do.
questions.explanation: Steam and boiling water can cause bad burns. Lifting the lid away from your body keeps your face and arms out of the hot steam. Young children should ask an adult to do this.

questions.title: States of Matter: Evaporation, Condensation, Boiling and Melting
questions.stem: A climber camps near the top of Mount Everest. Water there boils at only about 70 °C. Why does her rice take so long to cook?
options: Rice cannot soak up water when the air is cold.
There is no water vapour in the air on a mountain.
Boiling water on a mountain is hotter than 100 °C.
The boiling water is cooler than 100 °C, so it cooks the rice more slowly.
questions.explanation: On Everest the air pressure is low, so water boils at about 70 °C instead of 100 °C. Bubbling water that is only 70 °C is not hot enough to cook rice quickly.

questions.title: States of Matter: Evaporation, Condensation, Boiling and Melting
questions.stem: In the simulation, what do the particles do when water is a solid?

sim.task: Open States of Matter Basics and choose the States screen. Choose water, then press the Solid button. Watch the particles for a few seconds.

options: They fly around quickly and far apart.
They slide past each other.
They stay in a fixed pattern and only vibrate.
They stop and do not move at all.
questions.explanation: In a solid the particles are packed in a regular pattern and can only vibrate on the spot. That is why a solid keeps its shape.

questions.title: States of Matter: Evaporation, Condensation, Boiling and Melting
questions.stem: In the simulation, when you add more heat to the water, the particles move faster and the temperature on the thermometer goes up.

sim.task: Open States of Matter Basics and choose the States screen. Choose water and press Liquid. Slowly move the heat/cool control to add heat. Watch how fast the particles move and read the thermometer.

questions.explanation: Heat makes particles move faster, and the thermometer shows a higher temperature. Add enough heat and the liquid changes into a gas.

questions.title: States of Matter: Evaporation, Condensation, Boiling and Melting
questions.stem: Start with water as a solid and keep adding heat. Put what you see in order.

sim.task: Open States of Matter Basics and choose the States screen. Choose water and press Solid. Then add heat a little at a time with the heat/cool control, and press Liquid and Gas to compare what the particles do.

sequence: The particles vibrate in fixed places.
The particles break free and slide around each other.
The particles zoom around, far apart.
questions.explanation: Heating makes the particles move faster and faster: solid, then liquid, then gas.

questions.title: States of Matter: Evaporation, Condensation, Boiling and Melting
questions.stem: Class 5A heated ice and recorded the temperature every 2 minutes (example results). Time in minutes: 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14. Temperature in °C: −10, 0, 0, 25, 58, 90, 100, 100. In which 2-minute period did the temperature rise the most?
options: 0 to 2 minutes
6 to 8 minutes
4 to 6 minutes
8 to 10 minutes
questions.explanation: The rises were: 0–2 min +10 °C, 4–6 min +25 °C, 6–8 min +33 °C and 8–10 min +32 °C. The biggest rise was 6 to 8 minutes. The flat parts (2–4 and 12–14 minutes) are melting and boiling.

questions.title: States of Matter: Evaporation, Condensation, Boiling and Melting
questions.stem: Tuli watches a boiling kettle. Just above the spout there is a clear gap, and higher up there is a white cloud. What is in the clear gap?
options: invisible water vapour
tiny ice crystals
tiny drops of liquid water
empty space with nothing in it
questions.explanation: Water vapour is a gas and cannot be seen. As it moves away from the spout it cools and condenses into tiny drops of liquid water, and these drops make the white cloud we call steam.

questions.title: States of Matter: Evaporation, Condensation, Boiling and Melting
questions.stem: Sea water holds about 3.5 kg of salt in every 100 litres (example numbers). Three salt fields each hold 20 000 litres of sea water. If all the water evaporates, the three fields can make ___ kg of salt.
questions.explanation: One field has 20 000 ÷ 100 = 200 lots of 100 litres, so 200 × 3.5 = 700 kg. Three fields make 3 × 700 = 2100 kg. The salt does not evaporate, so all of it is left behind.

questions.title: States of Matter: Evaporation, Condensation, Boiling and Melting
questions.stem: A beaker of ice and water is heated steadily. The thermometer reads 0 °C for several minutes while the ice melts, even though the burner is still on. Explain why the temperature does not rise.
questions.model_answer: The heat energy is being used to melt the ice (to change it from solid to liquid), not to make the water warmer. When all the ice has melted, the temperature starts to rise again.
questions.explanation: During a change of state, the heat that is added is used to change the state, not to raise the temperature. The same happens at 100 °C while water boils.

questions.title: States of Matter: Evaporation, Condensation, Boiling and Melting
questions.stem: Joy tests whether a wide dish dries faster than a narrow cup. She leaves the dish in the sun for 4 hours with 100 ml of water. She leaves the cup in the shade for 2 hours with 50 ml of water. Which changes would make her test fair? Choose all that are right.
options: Put both containers in the same sunny place.
Start with the same volume of water in each.
Use a dish and a cup of the same width.
Leave both for the same length of time.
Use salty water in one and fresh water in the other.
questions.explanation: In a fair test only one thing changes (the surface area) and everything else stays the same: place, starting volume and time. Using the same width would remove the thing she is testing.

questions.title: Mixtures, Solutions and Changes
questions.stem: A **mixture** is…
options: two or more materials mixed together but not joined
a liquid with nothing at all in it
one material that has been heated and cooled
a solid that has changed into a liquid
questions.explanation: In a mixture the materials are only mixed, not joined, so each one keeps its own properties. That is why we can often separate them again.

questions.title: Mixtures, Solutions and Changes
questions.stem: Match each mixture to the best way to separate it.
questions.explanation: Choose a method that uses a difference between the materials: size (sieve), magnetism (magnet), insoluble solid in a liquid (filter), or a dissolved solid in a liquid (evaporate the water).

questions.title: Mixtures, Solutions and Changes
questions.stem: When sugar dissolves in water, it disappears and is gone for ever.
questions.explanation: The sugar breaks up into pieces too small to see and spreads through the water. It is still there: the water tastes sweet, and you can get the sugar back by evaporating the water.

questions.title: Mixtures, Solutions and Changes
questions.stem: Sort these materials into those that dissolve in water and those that do not.
questions.explanation: Salt, sugar and instant coffee dissolve to make solutions. Sand, chalk and flour stay as solid pieces in the water, so they can be filtered out.

questions.title: Mixtures, Solutions and Changes
questions.stem: Sort these changes into reversible and irreversible.
questions.explanation: Melting, freezing and dissolving can be undone because no new material is made. Baking, burning and rusting make new materials, so they cannot be undone.

questions.title: Mixtures, Solutions and Changes
questions.stem: Rana spilled sand, salt and iron nails into one jar. Put the steps in the best order to get all three back.
sequence: Use a magnet to pull out the iron nails.
Add water and stir so that the salt dissolves.
Filter the mixture: the sand stays in the filter paper.
Evaporate the water from the salty water to get the salt.
questions.explanation: Take out the magnetic nails first. Water dissolves the salt but not the sand, so filtering separates them. Evaporating the water from the filtered solution leaves the salt.

questions.title: Mixtures, Solutions and Changes
questions.stem: Which of these are signs that a new material has been made? Choose all that are right.
options: bubbles of gas appear
a new colour forms
heat or light is given out
the material is cut into smaller pieces
the material is stirred
questions.explanation: Bubbles of gas, a colour change, a new smell, and heat or light being given out all show that new materials are forming. Cutting and stirring only change the shape or position of a material.

questions.title: Mixtures, Solutions and Changes
questions.stem: Materials that dissolve in water are called ___, and materials that do not dissolve are called ___.
questions.explanation: Salt and sugar are soluble. Sand and chalk are insoluble. The liquid that forms when a solid dissolves is called a solution.

questions.title: Mixtures, Solutions and Changes
questions.stem: When salt dissolves in water we get a salt ___. The salt is still there, so the mass of the solution is the mass of the water ___ the mass of the salt.
questions.explanation: Dissolved salt is not lost. It is spread through the water, so the solution has a mass equal to the water plus the salt.

questions.title: Mixtures, Solutions and Changes
questions.stem: Salty water goes straight through filter paper, salt and all. Why?
options: The salt has changed into water.
The salt is so heavy that it sinks through the paper.
The dissolved salt is in pieces far too small to be caught by the paper.
The holes in the filter paper are too big for water.
questions.explanation: When salt dissolves it breaks into pieces much smaller than the holes in the filter paper. To get the salt back, evaporate the water instead.

questions.title: Mixtures, Solutions and Changes
questions.stem: Sumi says: 'When sugar dissolves in water it disappears, so it is gone.' Give two pieces of evidence that the sugar is still there.
questions.model_answer: The water tastes sweet. If you evaporate the water, the sugar is left behind. The solution weighs the same as the water plus the sugar.
questions.explanation: Taste, evaporating the water and measuring the mass all show that the sugar is still present in the solution, even though we cannot see it.

questions.title: Mixtures, Solutions and Changes
questions.stem: Which of these is an irreversible change?
options: melting chocolate
burning a match
dissolving salt in water
freezing juice
questions.explanation: Burning makes new materials (ash, gases, heat and light) and cannot be undone. Melting, dissolving and freezing can all be reversed.

questions.title: Mixtures, Solutions and Changes
questions.stem: Look at the picture of filtering muddy water. Which number shows the sand left behind (the residue)?
questions.image_alt: Filtering muddy water with a funnel and filter paper, with five parts numbered.
questions.explanation: Number 3 is the sand left behind in the filter paper. The clear water that passes through is number 4.

questions.title: Mixtures, Solutions and Changes
questions.stem: Use the picture of the filtering equipment. Put the steps for filtering sandy water in order.
questions.image_alt: A funnel with filter paper over a beaker, with sand left in the paper and clear water in the beaker.
sequence: Fold the filter paper and put it in the funnel.
Stand the funnel over a beaker.
Pour the sandy water slowly into the funnel.
Clear water drips into the beaker and the sand stays in the paper.
questions.explanation: The filter paper must be in place before you pour. The liquid passes through the tiny holes in the paper, but the insoluble sand is too big and stays behind.

questions.title: Mixtures, Solutions and Changes
questions.stem: Sort the pictures into reversible and irreversible changes.
questions.explanation: Melting and dissolving can be undone by cooling or evaporating. Cooking an egg, bread or rice makes new materials, and you can never turn them back into the raw food.

questions.title: Mixtures, Solutions and Changes
questions.stem: Which tool is best for pulling iron nails out of a pile of sand?
questions.explanation: Iron is magnetic and sand is not, so a magnet pulls out only the nails. Scissors, a spoon or a magnifying glass cannot tell the two materials apart.

questions.title: Mixtures, Solutions and Changes
questions.stem: Rana pours sandy salt water into the funnel in the picture. What collects in the beaker (5)?
questions.image_alt: Filtering with a funnel, filter paper, sand left behind and a beaker of clear liquid below.
options: pure water with no salt
sandy water
salty water with no sand
dry salt crystals
questions.explanation: The sand is insoluble and stays in the filter paper. The salt is dissolved in tiny pieces and goes through with the water, so the beaker holds salty water.

questions.title: Mixtures, Solutions and Changes
questions.stem: Which of these will dissolve in water?
questions.explanation: Salt is soluble, so it dissolves in water to make a solution. Rock, brick and wood are insoluble.

questions.title: Mixtures, Solutions and Changes
questions.stem: Farmers toss rice in a flat bamboo tray called a kula, in the breeze. The grains fall back into the tray but the husks blow away. Why?
options: The tray has holes that only the husks can fit through.
The husks dissolve in the moving air.
The grains are magnetic and are pulled back to the tray.
The wind blows the light husks away, but the heavy grains fall back.
questions.explanation: Rice grains and husks have different masses. The wind can carry the light husks, but the heavier grains fall straight back down.

questions.title: Mixtures, Solutions and Changes
questions.stem: Nadia stirs a spoon of sugar into her hot cha and the sugar seems to disappear. Where is the sugar now?
options: It has changed into water.
It has dissolved and is spread through the cha.
It has floated to the top of the cha.
It has been destroyed.
questions.explanation: Dissolved sugar is broken into tiny pieces that spread through the liquid. The cha tastes sweet because the sugar is still there.

questions.title: Mixtures, Solutions and Changes
questions.stem: Moung filters muddy pond water through a clean cloth and the water looks clear. It is now safe to drink.
questions.explanation: Filtering removes mud and other solid pieces. Germs and dissolved substances are far too small to be caught by the cloth, so the water still needs to be boiled or properly treated.

questions.title: Mixtures, Solutions and Changes
questions.stem: On a winter morning in Jashore, a neighbour offers Arif a cup of fresh, raw date palm sap that was filtered through cloth. What should Arif do?
options: Drink it, because the cloth has removed everything harmful.
Leave it in a warm place for a few hours and drink it later.
Drink just a small sip, to test it.
Say no politely, and say that sap should be boiled before anyone drinks it.
questions.explanation: Cloth can remove insects and bark, but a virus is far too small to be stopped by it. Health experts in Bangladesh say never to drink raw date palm sap, because bats can contaminate it. Boiling makes it safe.

questions.title: Mixtures, Solutions and Changes
questions.stem: Rafi bakes a cake. After it has cooled, he can change it back into flour, eggs and sugar.
questions.explanation: Baking makes new materials. The cake rises because gas bubbles form, the colour and smell change, and the ingredients cannot be taken back out. It is an irreversible change.

questions.title: Mixtures, Solutions and Changes
questions.stem: Priya wants one spoon of sugar to dissolve quickly in a glass of water. Which actions will help? Choose all that are right.
options: stir the water
use fine sugar instead of big lumps
use warmer water
leave it without stirring
use bigger sugar crystals
questions.explanation: Stirring, smaller pieces and warmer water all make dissolving faster. Leaving it still or using big crystals slows it down.

questions.title: Mixtures, Solutions and Changes
questions.stem: Class 5B timed how long one teaspoon of sugar took to dissolve in 100 ml of water at different temperatures (example results). At 10 °C it took 180 s, at 25 °C 95 s, at 40 °C 50 s and at 60 °C 25 s. What is the best prediction for the time at 50 °C?
options: about 15 seconds
about 35 seconds
about 75 seconds
about 100 seconds
questions.explanation: The time falls as the water gets warmer. 50 °C lies between 40 °C (50 s) and 60 °C (25 s), so the time must lie between 25 s and 50 s: about 35 seconds.

questions.title: Mixtures, Solutions and Changes
questions.stem: Using the same results (10 °C: 180 s, 25 °C: 95 s, 40 °C: 50 s, 60 °C: 25 s), the sugar took ___ seconds longer to dissolve at 10 °C than at 60 °C.
questions.explanation: 180 − 25 = 155 seconds. Cold water dissolves sugar much more slowly than hot water.

questions.title: Mixtures, Solutions and Changes
questions.stem: Class 5B timed each temperature only once. How could they make their results more reliable?
questions.model_answer: Repeat the test at each temperature several times (for example three times) and work out the average (mean) time.
questions.explanation: One result might be wrong because of a mistake or a slow stopwatch. Repeating the test and finding the average makes the results more reliable.
