questions.title: Mixtures, Solutions and Changes
questions.stem: Joy puts 200 g of water in a cup and stirs in 15 g of salt until it has all dissolved (example numbers). The salty water has a mass of ___ g.
questions.explanation: The salt is still there, just spread through the water, so the masses add: 200 + 15 = 215 g.

questions.title: Mixtures, Solutions and Changes
questions.stem: Rafi mixes iron filings, chalk powder and sugar. He stirs the mixture into water and filters it. What is left on the filter paper?
options: iron filings and sugar
sugar and chalk powder
iron filings and chalk powder
only chalk powder
questions.explanation: Sugar is soluble, so it dissolves and goes through the paper with the water. Iron filings and chalk are insoluble and stay behind. Rafi could then use a magnet to pull out the iron.

questions.title: Mixtures, Solutions and Changes
questions.stem: Imran says: 'A burning candle is just wax melting, so the change is reversible.' Which observation shows that this is not the whole story?
options: The flame gives out heat and light and the candle slowly gets smaller.
The wax near the flame is soft and runny.
The melted wax goes hard again when it cools.
The candle is made from a solid material.
questions.explanation: Melted wax that sets again is reversible. But burning also uses up wax to make new substances and gives out heat and light, and that part cannot be undone.

questions.title: Matter, Atoms and Conservation
questions.stem: All matter is made of tiny building blocks called…
options: cells
atoms
droplets
crystals
questions.explanation: Air, water, your desk and your body are all made of atoms. Atoms are so small that a single human hair is about half a million atoms wide.

questions.title: Matter, Atoms and Conservation
questions.stem: A material made of only one kind of atom is an ___. When atoms join together they make a ___.
questions.explanation: Oxygen, iron and gold are elements. A water molecule is two hydrogen atoms joined to one oxygen atom.

questions.title: Matter, Atoms and Conservation
questions.stem: Match each key word to its meaning.
pairs: the tiny building block of matter
made of only one kind of atom
nothing can get in or out
questions.explanation: These key words describe matter and how we study it. The nucleus holds the protons and neutrons, with the electrons moving around it.

questions.title: Matter, Atoms and Conservation
questions.stem: When sugar dissolves in water, its atoms are destroyed.
questions.explanation: No atoms are destroyed in any physical or chemical change. The sugar atoms are still there, spread through the water.

questions.title: Matter, Atoms and Conservation
questions.stem: 330 g of juice is frozen to make an ice lolly. The ice lolly has a mass of ___ g.
questions.explanation: Freezing only rearranges how the particles are arranged. No atoms are gained or lost, so the mass stays at 330 g.

questions.title: Matter, Atoms and Conservation
questions.stem: Sort these into elements and substances made of different atoms joined together.
questions.explanation: Iron, gold and aluminium are each made of only one kind of atom. Water has hydrogen and oxygen atoms joined, and carbon dioxide has carbon and oxygen atoms joined.

questions.title: Matter, Atoms and Conservation
questions.stem: Which of these is a closed system?
options: an open pan of boiling water
a candle burning in a room
a puddle drying in the sun
a sealed jar
questions.explanation: In a closed system nothing can get in or out. A sealed jar keeps everything inside, while open pans, candles and puddles can lose gases to the air.

questions.title: Matter, Atoms and Conservation
questions.stem: Vinegar and baking soda react in a sealed bag and the bag puffs up with gas. Which of these stay the same? Choose all that are right.
options: the total number of atoms
the total mass of the bag and its contents
the kinds of atom present
the substances inside the bag
the way the atoms are joined together
questions.explanation: In a chemical change atoms are rearranged but none are made or destroyed, so the atom count, the kinds of atom and the total mass stay the same. The substances and how atoms are joined do change.

questions.title: Matter, Atoms and Conservation
questions.stem: What happens to the total amount of energy in a closed system?
options: The total stays the same; energy only moves or changes form.
Energy is made new whenever something moves.
The energy slowly disappears into the air.
Some energy is destroyed every time it changes form.
questions.explanation: Energy cannot be made or destroyed. It moves from place to place or changes form, for example from electrical energy to light and heat.

questions.title: Matter, Atoms and Conservation
questions.stem: A candle has a mass of 50 g. After burning for an hour its mass is 42 g. Has mass been destroyed? Explain.
questions.model_answer: No. The wax reacted with oxygen and turned into carbon dioxide gas and water vapour, which escaped into the air because the candle was in an open system.
questions.explanation: The atoms of wax were rearranged into gases that drifted into the air, so the candle lost mass. If you caught all the gases in a sealed container, the total mass would not change.

questions.title: Matter, Atoms and Conservation
questions.stem: Class 5C want to check whether mass is conserved in a reaction. Which tool do they need?
questions.explanation: A balance measures mass. The class weigh everything before the reaction and again after, then compare the two readings.

questions.title: Matter, Atoms and Conservation
questions.stem: Which of these gets its heat from splitting big uranium atoms?
questions.explanation: In a nuclear power plant, uranium atoms are split into smaller atoms of other elements, which gives out a huge amount of heat. A campfire and a candle burn fuel, which is a chemical change.

questions.title: Matter, Atoms and Conservation
questions.stem: Match each picture to what happens to its atoms.
pairs: small hydrogen atoms join to make helium
big uranium atoms split into smaller atoms
atoms rearrange into gases, smoke and ash
the same molecules, just moving around more
questions.explanation: Nuclear changes in the Sun and in a power plant change the nucleus, so one element turns into another. Burning rearranges atoms, and melting only changes how the molecules move.

questions.title: Matter, Atoms and Conservation
questions.stem: Sort the pictures into physical, chemical and nuclear changes.

items.text: uranium atoms splitting in a power plant
hydrogen atoms joining in the Sun

questions.explanation: In a physical change atoms just move around. In a chemical change atoms are rearranged to make new substances. In a nuclear change the nucleus itself changes.

questions.title: Matter, Atoms and Conservation
questions.stem: Put the steps of making electricity in a nuclear power station in order.

sequence.text: Uranium atoms split in the reactor.
A lot of heat is released.
The heat boils water into steam.
The turbine turns a generator, making electricity.

questions.explanation: Splitting uranium atoms releases heat. The heat makes steam, the steam spins the turbine, and the turbine drives the generator. Energy changes form at each step, but none is lost.

questions.title: Matter, Atoms and Conservation
questions.stem: The picture shows water as a solid, a liquid and a gas. Changing from one box to the next only changes how the particles are arranged and move. No atoms are lost or made.
questions.image_alt: Three boxes of water particles: solid on the left (packed in rows), liquid in the middle (touching), gas on the right (far apart), joined by arrows labelled melting, freezing, evaporating and condensing.
questions.explanation: Melting, freezing, evaporating and condensing are physical changes. The same atoms are present in every box, just arranged and moving differently.

questions.title: Matter, Atoms and Conservation
questions.stem: Nadia boils water in an open pot. After 20 minutes the pot and water weigh less. Where did the missing mass go?
options: It sank into the bottom of the pot.
The water was destroyed.
It turned into rice.
It escaped into the air as water vapour.
questions.explanation: Boiling turns liquid water into water vapour, which drifts away from the open pot. No atoms are destroyed; they are just in the air now.

questions.title: Matter, Atoms and Conservation
questions.stem: Rafi weighs a shiny iron nail. After some weeks in a damp place it is covered in rust and weighs a little more. Where does the extra mass come from?
options: The nail makes new iron atoms.
The rust is lighter, so the nail should weigh less.
Iron atoms join with oxygen (and water) from the air.
A bit of dust settles on the nail.
questions.explanation: Rust is a new substance made when iron atoms join with oxygen from the air. The added atoms add mass. Nothing is created from nothing.

questions.title: Matter, Atoms and Conservation
questions.stem: Tuli makes sherbet by stirring 20 g of sugar into 250 g of water. She says the sherbet should have a mass of 270 g.
questions.explanation: The sugar dissolves but its atoms are still there. The mass of the solution is the water plus the sugar: 250 g + 20 g = 270 g.

questions.title: Matter, Atoms and Conservation
questions.stem: Class 5C react vinegar and baking soda in a zip-lock bag on a balance. What is the safest way to do the experiment?
options: Smell the gas closely to check what it is.
Wear goggles and point the bag away from faces.
Taste the mixture to see what it is like.
Squeeze the bag hard so that it fizzes more.
questions.explanation: Vinegar can sting eyes, and a puffed-up bag could burst. Goggles and pointing the bag away keep everyone safe. We never taste or sniff closely in science.

questions.title: Matter, Atoms and Conservation
questions.stem: Bangladesh is building its first nuclear power plant at Rooppur, beside the Padma. Which of these are advantages of nuclear power? Choose all that are right.
options: a lot of energy from a little fuel
almost no carbon dioxide while the plant works
steady power day and night
used fuel stays radioactive for thousands of years
it is very expensive to build
questions.explanation: Nuclear plants give a lot of energy from a small amount of uranium and almost no carbon dioxide, and they run day and night. The last two choices are disadvantages.

questions.title: Matter, Atoms and Conservation
questions.stem: In the simulation, you give the sandwich maker far more cheese than the recipe can use. What do you see in the After box?

sim.task: Open Reactants, Products and Leftovers and choose the Sandwiches screen. Pick a recipe. In the Before box, use the sliders to give a large number of cheese slices and only a few of the other ingredients. Look at the After box.

options: The extra cheese disappears.
The sandwich maker makes more sandwiches than the recipe allows.
The extra cheese turns into bread.
Some cheese is left over after the sandwiches are made.
questions.explanation: Each sandwich needs a fixed amount of each ingredient. Ingredients that are not used up are the leftovers. Nothing disappears.

questions.title: Matter, Atoms and Conservation
questions.stem: In the simulation, the slices of bread you start with always equal the slices of bread in the sandwiches plus the bread slices left over.

sim.task: Open Reactants, Products and Leftovers and choose the Sandwiches screen. Pick a recipe and set the number of bread, cheese and meat slices in the Before box. Count the bread slices before. Then count the bread in the sandwiches plus any bread left over after. Try two different settings.

questions.explanation: The sandwich model shows conservation: ingredients (like atoms) are only rearranged into sandwiches, and the ones not used are leftovers. None are made or lost.

questions.title: Matter, Atoms and Conservation
questions.stem: In the sandwich model, match each science word to what it means.

sim.task: Open Reactants, Products and Leftovers and choose the Sandwiches screen. Look at the Before box and the After box and think about what each one shows.

pairs: ingredients that are not used up
questions.explanation: In a chemical reaction the reactants are rearranged to make products. Any reactant that is not used up is a leftover.

questions.title: Matter, Atoms and Conservation
questions.stem: Example: a nucleus with 235 protons and neutrons is hit by 1 free neutron, then splits into pieces with 139 and 94 protons and neutrons, plus 3 free neutrons. Before: 235 + 1 = ___. After: 139 + 94 + 3 = ___.
questions.explanation: Both totals are 236, so the total number of protons plus neutrons is conserved, even though one element has changed into others.

questions.title: Matter, Atoms and Conservation
questions.stem: Example: a nucleus with 236 protons and neutrons splits into two pieces with 140 and 94 protons and neutrons, and some free neutrons. If the total number of protons and neutrons is conserved, how many free neutrons are released?
questions.explanation: The two pieces have 140 + 94 = 234. To reach the original 236, there must be 236 − 234 = 2 free neutrons.

questions.title: Matter, Atoms and Conservation
questions.stem: Which statement about chemical changes and nuclear changes is correct?
options: Atoms are not conserved in either kind of change.
Atoms are conserved in both chemical changes and nuclear changes.
In chemical changes atoms are only rearranged, but in nuclear changes one kind of atom changes into another.
Nothing at all is conserved in a nuclear change.
questions.explanation: Chemical changes rearrange the same atoms. Nuclear changes alter the nucleus, so one element becomes another. Even so, the total number of protons plus neutrons stays the same.

questions.title: Matter, Atoms and Conservation
questions.stem: Class 5C measured mass before and after (example results). Salt dissolving in an open cup: 270 g then 270 g. Vinegar and baking soda in a sealed bag: 312 g then 312 g. The same reaction in an open cup: 312 g then 309 g. What best explains the 3 g lost from the open cup?
options: A gas made in the reaction escaped into the air.
Atoms were destroyed, but only in an open cup.
The balance gives lower readings when a cup is open.
The salt dissolving took away some mass.
questions.explanation: The reaction made a gas (carbon dioxide). In the sealed bag the gas could not escape, so the mass stayed 312 g. In the open cup the gas escaped, taking 3 g of mass with it.

questions.title: Matter, Atoms and Conservation
questions.stem: Explain why scientists say atoms are conserved in chemical changes but not in nuclear changes, and say what is still conserved in a nuclear change.
questions.model_answer: In chemical changes atoms are only rearranged, so the same atoms are there before and after. In nuclear changes the nucleus changes, so atoms of one element turn into another. The total number of protons plus neutrons is still the same.
questions.explanation: Chemical changes only move atoms into new groups. Nuclear changes alter the atoms themselves, but counting all the protons and neutrons gives the same total before and after.

questions.title: Matter, Atoms and Conservation
questions.stem: Example: of every 10 units of electrical energy a light bulb uses, 2 units become light. In a closed system the other ___ units must become heat.
questions.explanation: Energy is conserved: the total must stay at 10 units. 10 − 2 = 8 units, so 8 units become heat.

questions.title: Energy and Its Transformations
questions.stem: Which form of energy is stored in food?
options: chemical
electrical
light
sound
questions.explanation: Food, fuel and batteries store chemical energy. Our bodies change the chemical energy in food into movement and heat.

questions.title: Energy and Its Transformations
questions.stem: Sort these by the main form of energy they have or give out.
questions.explanation: Moving things have kinetic energy. Food and batteries store chemical energy. A firefly gives out light and a drum gives out sound.

questions.title: Energy and Its Transformations
questions.stem: Match each device to the energy change it makes.
questions.explanation: Every device transforms energy from one form into another. Some of the energy always ends up as heat that we do not need.

questions.title: Energy and Its Transformations
questions.stem: Energy cannot be created or ___. It can only move from place to place or change ___.
questions.explanation: This is the law of conservation of energy. The total amount of energy stays the same; it is only moved or transformed.

questions.title: Energy and Its Transformations
questions.stem: Heat moves from a hotter object to a colder object.
questions.explanation: Heat is energy that always flows from hotter things to colder things. That is why a hot cup of tea cools down until it reaches room temperature.

questions.title: Energy and Its Transformations
questions.stem: A ball bounces lower and lower and then stops. Where has its energy gone?
options: It was destroyed when the ball stopped moving.
It spread out as heat and sound.
It is still inside the ball as movement energy.
It was changed into light energy that we cannot see.
questions.explanation: Energy cannot be destroyed. Each time the ball hits the ground, some of its energy spreads out as heat and sound, so the ball has less energy for bouncing.

questions.title: Energy and Its Transformations
questions.stem: Which of these materials are good thermal insulators? Choose all that are right.
options: wood
wool
plastic
iron
copper
questions.explanation: Insulators such as wood, wool, plastic and trapped air slow heat down. Metals like iron and copper are thermal conductors that let heat pass easily.

questions.title: Energy and Its Transformations
questions.stem: A solar panel changes ___ energy into ___ energy.
questions.explanation: Sunlight shining on a solar panel is changed into electrical energy. A little heat is given out too.

questions.title: Energy and Its Transformations
questions.stem: An LED bulb is more efficient than an old filament bulb because it wastes less energy as heat.
questions.explanation: An LED bulb gives the same light as a filament bulb but uses only about one fifth of the electricity. More of its energy becomes light and less is wasted as heat.

questions.title: Energy and Its Transformations
questions.stem: Explain why a metal spoon in hot tea gets hot quickly, but a wooden spoon does not.
questions.model_answer: Metal is a thermal conductor, so heat moves through it easily. Wood is a thermal insulator, so heat moves through it slowly.
questions.explanation: Metals are thermal conductors and carry heat along them quickly. Wood slows heat down, so the end you hold stays cool for much longer.

questions.title: Energy and Its Transformations
questions.stem: When a ceiling fan is switched off, its energy has been destroyed.
questions.explanation: Energy is never destroyed. When the fan stops, its movement energy has spread out into the surroundings, mostly as heat and sound.

questions.title: Energy and Its Transformations
questions.stem: The four cups hold the same hot water. One is uncovered and the others are wrapped in newspaper, wool or foil. Which cup would you expect to stay hot the longest?
questions.image_alt: Four cups of hot water: one with no cover and the others wrapped in newspaper, wool and foil.
options: the uncovered cup
the cup wrapped in newspaper
the cup wrapped in foil
the cup wrapped in wool
questions.explanation: Wool traps lots of air, and air is a poor conductor of heat, so heat escapes slowly. It is the best insulator of these materials.

questions.title: Energy and Its Transformations
questions.stem: In this fair test of four cups, which cup is the control that the others are compared with?
questions.image_alt: Four cups of hot water: one with no cover and the others wrapped in newspaper, wool and foil.
options: the cup in wool
the cup in newspaper
the uncovered cup
the cup in foil
questions.explanation: The uncovered cup shows how fast hot water cools with no insulation at all. It is the comparison for the three wrapped cups.

questions.title: Energy and Its Transformations
questions.stem: Match each picture to the main energy it gives out.
questions.explanation: A loudspeaker gives out sound, a bulb gives out light, a fan makes air move and a hot drink gives out heat.

questions.title: Energy and Its Transformations
questions.stem: Sort the pictures into things that are moving and things that store energy.
questions.explanation: Moving things have kinetic energy. Batteries, food and fuels such as wood store chemical energy until it is released.

questions.title: Energy and Its Transformations
questions.stem: Which picture shows a device that changes sunlight into electricity?
questions.explanation: A solar panel changes light energy from the Sun into electrical energy. A wind turbine uses moving air, and candles and kettles use chemical or electrical energy.

questions.title: Energy and Its Transformations
questions.stem: The three thermometers show the temperatures of three cups of water. Cup A and cup C are placed touching in a closed box. Which way does heat move?
questions.image_alt: Three thermometers A, B and C reading 12 °C, 37 °C and 48 °C.
options: from cup A to cup C
from cup C to cup A
nowhere, because both are water
in both directions equally
questions.explanation: Cup C (48 °C) is hotter than cup A (12 °C), so heat moves from C to A. Cup C loses heat and cools, and cup A gains heat and warms, until they are the same temperature.

questions.title: Energy and Its Transformations
questions.stem: Rafi eats a plate of rice and then pedals his rickshaw all day. Which energy chain describes this?
options: kinetic (food) → chemical (rickshaw) + heat
light (food) → electrical (rickshaw) + sound
chemical (food) → kinetic (rickshaw) + heat
electrical (food) → sound (rickshaw) + light
questions.explanation: The chemical energy stored in food is changed into movement energy, and some becomes heat. This is why we feel warm when we work hard.

questions.title: Energy and Its Transformations
questions.stem: Cooking pots in many kitchens are made of metal, but their handles are made of wood or plastic. Why?
options: Wood and plastic are insulators, so the handle stays cool.
Wood and plastic are conductors, so heat reaches the food faster.
Metal handles would be too heavy, so the pot would tip over.
Wood and plastic make the food inside heat up more quickly.
questions.explanation: Metal is a good thermal conductor, so heat passes quickly from the flame to the food. Wood and plastic are insulators and slow heat down, which keeps the handle safe to hold.

questions.title: Energy and Its Transformations
questions.stem: A village home in Bangladesh has a solar home system. Put the energy steps in order, from day to night.
sequence: Sunlight shines on the solar panel on the roof.
The panel changes the light energy into electrical energy.
The battery stores the energy as chemical energy.
At night the battery supplies electrical energy.
The LED light changes the electrical energy into light (and a little heat).
questions.explanation: The panel works in the daytime and the battery stores the energy for the night. At every step energy is changed in form and a little is wasted as heat, but none is destroyed.

questions.title: Energy and Its Transformations
questions.stem: Mina wants her soup to stay hot until lunch. Which of these will help? Choose all that are right.
options: put it in an insulated flask
wrap the container in a woollen cloth
keep the lid on
leave the lid off in a cool breeze
pour it into a thin metal cup
questions.explanation: Insulators such as a flask, wool and a lid slow the loss of heat. An open lid in a breeze and a thin metal cup let heat escape quickly.

questions.title: Energy and Its Transformations
questions.stem: A metal spoon has been left in a pot on the stove. Tuli says it is safe to grab it with bare hands because metal stays cool.
questions.explanation: Metal is a thermal conductor, so heat travels quickly along the spoon and it becomes very hot. Use a dry cloth or pot holder, which are insulators, and take care.

questions.title: Energy and Its Transformations
questions.stem: Put the energy changes in order for the cyclist lighting a bulb.

sim.task: Open Energy Forms and Changes and choose the Systems screen. Choose the cyclist as the energy source, the generator as the energy changer and the light bulb as the energy user. Switch the cyclist on and watch the energy symbols move.

sequence: The cyclist changes chemical energy from food into movement of the pedals.
The pedals turn the generator.
The generator changes movement energy into electrical energy.
The bulb changes the electrical energy into light and heat.
questions.explanation: Energy moves along the chain and changes form at each step. The bulb gives out light and some heat, and the total energy stays the same.

questions.title: Energy and Its Transformations
questions.stem: What happens to the temperature of the water in the beaker?

sim.task: Open Energy Forms and Changes and choose the Intro screen. Drag the beaker of water above one of the burners. Slide the burner control up to Heat for a while and watch the thermometer. Then slide it down to Cool for a while and watch again.

options: It falls when heated and rises when it is cooled.
It rises when heated and falls when cooled.
It stays the same either way.
It rises both when heated and when cooled.
questions.explanation: When the water gains heat its temperature rises, and when it loses heat its temperature falls.

questions.title: Energy and Its Transformations
questions.stem: What happens to the atoms and the temperature as you rub the books together?

sim.task: Open Friction. Drag the top book so that it rubs back and forth across the bottom book for a while. Watch the atoms and the thermometer.

options: The atoms jiggle faster and the temperature rises.
The atoms stop moving and the temperature stays the same.
The atoms jiggle slower and the temperature falls.
The atoms disappear and the temperature falls.
questions.explanation: Your movement energy is transferred to the atoms, which jiggle faster. Faster-moving atoms mean the books are warmer: movement energy has changed into thermal energy.

questions.title: Energy and Its Transformations
questions.stem: Class 5D poured 200 ml of water at 80 °C into identical cups (example results). After 20 minutes the temperatures were: no cover 52 °C, newspaper 60 °C, wool 68 °C, foil 58 °C. The uncovered cup cooled by ___ °C more than the cup wrapped in wool.
questions.explanation: The uncovered cup cooled by 80 − 52 = 28 °C, and the wool cup by 80 − 68 = 12 °C. The difference is 28 − 12 = 16 °C. Wool is the best insulator.

questions.title: Energy and Its Transformations
questions.stem: A filament bulb uses 25 W. An LED bulb that gives the same light uses about one fifth as much (example numbers). Energy used (Wh) = power (W) × time (h). How much less electrical energy does the LED use in 4 hours?
options: 20 Wh
80 Wh
100 Wh
5 Wh
questions.explanation: The LED uses 25 ÷ 5 = 5 W. In 4 hours the filament bulb uses 25 × 4 = 100 Wh and the LED uses 5 × 4 = 20 Wh. The saving is 100 − 20 = 80 Wh, because the LED wastes much less energy as heat.

questions.title: Energy and Its Transformations
questions.stem: Energy (Wh) = power (W) × time (h). A 50 W solar panel gets 5 hours of good sunshine, so it makes 250 Wh a day (example numbers). A family uses three 5 W LED bulbs for 4 hours and a 20 W fan for 6 hours. How much energy is left to charge phones?
options: 130 Wh
70 Wh
180 Wh
250 Wh
questions.explanation: Bulbs: 3 × 5 × 4 = 60 Wh. Fan: 20 × 6 = 120 Wh. Total used 180 Wh. Energy left: 250 − 180 = 70 Wh, enough to charge a phone.

questions.title: Energy and Its Transformations
questions.stem: 'We should save energy, but energy cannot be destroyed.' Explain why both statements can be true.
questions.model_answer: Energy is never destroyed, but useful energy such as fuel or electricity gets changed into heat that spreads out and cannot be used again. Saving energy means using less of the limited useful energy, which costs money and may run out.
questions.explanation: The total amount of energy stays the same, but much of it ends up as spread-out heat that is no longer useful to us. Fuels are limited, so using less of them saves useful energy.

questions.title: Energy and Its Transformations
questions.stem: An uncovered cup of water cooled from 80 °C to 52 °C in 20 minutes (example data). The room stays at 30 °C all night. What will the temperature of the water be next morning?
options: about 52 °C
about 0 °C
about 80 °C
about 30 °C
questions.explanation: The water loses heat to the room until it reaches the same temperature as the room, 30 °C. It cannot become colder than the room without a fridge or ice.

questions.title: Sound
questions.stem: Every sound starts with a ___. It travels as a ___ and cannot travel through empty ___.
questions.explanation: A vibrating object pushes on the particles next to it, and the vibration passes along as a sound wave. In empty space there are no particles, so sound cannot travel.

questions.title: Sound
questions.stem: Match each sound source to the part that vibrates.
pairs: the vocal cords in your throat
questions.explanation: Hitting, plucking and blowing make different parts vibrate. When you hum, you can feel the vibration of your vocal cords with your fingers on your throat.

questions.title: Sound
questions.stem: Sound travels faster through steel than through air.
questions.explanation: Sound travels at about 340 metres per second in air, 1500 in water and 5900 in steel. Particles in solids are closer together, so they pass the vibrations on faster.

questions.title: Sound
questions.stem: Astronauts standing on the Moon can hear each other talk without radios.
questions.explanation: The Moon has no air, so there are no particles to pass the vibrations along. Sound cannot travel through empty space, so astronauts use radios.

questions.title: Sound
questions.stem: Sort these changes by what they do to the pitch of a string instrument.
questions.explanation: Short, tight, thin strings vibrate faster (a higher frequency), so they make a higher pitch. Long, loose, thick strings vibrate more slowly and make a lower pitch.

questions.title: Sound
questions.stem: Put the steps in order to show how you hear a sound.
sequence: The outer ear collects the sound.
The sound goes down the ear canal.
The eardrum vibrates.
Three tiny bones pass the vibrations on.
The cochlea turns them into messages.
A nerve carries the messages to the brain.
questions.explanation: The eardrum is a thin skin that vibrates when sound reaches it. The tiny bones pass the vibrations to the cochlea, which sends messages along a nerve to the brain.

questions.title: Sound
questions.stem: The number of vibrations each second is called the frequency. It is measured in…
options: decibels (dB)
metres per second
newtons
hertz (Hz)
questions.explanation: Frequency is measured in hertz (Hz). A frequency of 100 Hz means 100 vibrations every second. Decibels measure loudness, not pitch.

questions.title: Sound
questions.stem: Which of these would change the **pitch** of a guitar string? Choose all that are right.
options: making the string shorter
making the string tighter
using a thinner string
plucking the string harder
plucking the string gently
questions.explanation: Length, tightness and thickness change how fast the string vibrates, and so the pitch. Plucking harder or more gently only changes the size of the vibrations, which changes loudness.

questions.title: Sound
questions.stem: On a wave diagram, what shows how loud the sound is?
options: how long the diagram is
how close together the waves are
the height of the wave
the colour of the line
questions.explanation: Taller waves mean bigger vibrations and a louder sound. How close the waves are together shows the pitch.

questions.title: Sound
questions.stem: Why do we see lightning before we hear the thunder?
questions.model_answer: Light travels much faster than sound, so the light reaches us first and the sound arrives later.
questions.explanation: Light travels almost instantly, but sound travels at only about 340 metres per second in air. The further away the storm, the longer the gap.

questions.title: Sound
questions.stem: Which number is the eardrum, the thin skin that vibrates when sound reaches it?
questions.image_alt: A cross-section of the ear with parts numbered 1 to 6.
questions.explanation: Number 3 is the eardrum. It sits at the end of the ear canal (2) and vibrates when sound waves hit it.

questions.title: Sound
questions.stem: Which number is the part that turns vibrations into messages for the brain?
questions.image_alt: A cross-section of the ear with parts numbered 1 to 6.
questions.explanation: The cochlea (5) turns vibrations into messages. A nerve (6) then carries the messages to the brain. The tiny bones (4) only pass the vibrations on.

questions.title: Sound
questions.stem: Which wave shows the **quietest** sound with the **highest** pitch?
questions.image_alt: Four sound wave drawings A to D that differ in height and in how close the waves are.
options: A
B
C
D
questions.explanation: Short waves mean a quiet sound and waves close together mean a high pitch. Wave D has short waves that are close together.

questions.title: Sound
questions.stem: Look at the four wave pictures. Match each wave to the sound it shows.
questions.image_alt: Four sound wave drawings A to D that differ in height and in how close the waves are.
questions.explanation: Height shows loudness: A and C are tall (loud), B and D are short (quiet). Closeness shows pitch: C and D have waves close together (high), A and B have waves far apart (low).

questions.title: Sound
questions.stem: Use the decibel scale. Which sounds could damage hearing if you heard them for a long time? Choose all that are right.
questions.image_alt: A decibel scale from 0 to 140 with leaves 20 dB, birds 40, talking 60, traffic 80, loud music 100 and a plane 120. Sounds above 85 dB are shaded.
options: leaves rustling
talking
traffic
loud music
a plane taking off
questions.explanation: Sounds above about 85 dB can permanently damage hearing. Loud music (100 dB) and a plane (120 dB) are in the shaded danger zone. Traffic, at 80 dB, is just below it.

questions.title: Sound
questions.stem: Look at the three instruments. Which one makes its sound when the air inside it vibrates?
questions.image_alt: A dhol (drum), an ektara (string instrument) and a bansuri (flute).
options: the dhol (drum)
the bansuri (flute)
the ektara (string)
questions.explanation: In a bansuri, blowing across the hole makes the column of air inside vibrate. In the dhol it is the drum skin, and in the ektara it is the string.

questions.title: Sound
questions.stem: An ektara player squeezes the bamboo neck to make the string tighter. What happens to the pitch?
options: It gets higher, because the string vibrates faster.
It gets lower, because the string vibrates slower.
It gets louder, because the vibrations are bigger.
It stays the same, because the string has not got any shorter.
questions.explanation: A tighter string vibrates faster, so its frequency and pitch go up. Loudness depends on how hard the string is plucked.

questions.title: Sound
questions.stem: Whales can hear each other across hundreds of kilometres of ocean. Which fact helps to explain this?
options: Sound travels well and fast through water.
Whale calls travel through the air above the waves.
Light travels through the ocean at the same speed as sound.
Sound is slower in water than in air, so it lasts longer.
questions.explanation: The particles of water are close together, so they pass vibrations along quickly and sound carries a long way. Sound travels about 1500 metres per second in water compared with 340 in air.

questions.title: Sound
questions.stem: Rafi's friend listens to loud music through headphones for hours every day. What is the best advice?
options: Turn the volume up so that the quiet parts can be heard.
Keep the volume as it is, because ears get used to it.
Only music with a low pitch can harm hearing.
Turn the volume down and take breaks.
questions.explanation: Sounds louder than about 85 dB, heard for a long time, can permanently damage hearing. Ears do not get used to loud sound, and it is loudness, not pitch, that causes the harm.

questions.title: Sound
questions.stem: Bangladesh's noise rules make the areas around hospitals and schools silent zones with low noise limits, because loud noise can harm health and learning.
questions.explanation: Noise can cause hearing loss, headaches, stress and poor sleep, and it makes it harder for children to concentrate. Silent zones near hospitals and schools protect people, with limits as low as 50 dB in the daytime.

questions.title: Sound
questions.stem: A busy road runs past a school in Dhaka. Which actions would help to make a quiet school zone? Choose all that are right.
options: put up 'No horn' signs near the school
plant trees and build a wall beside the road
hang curtains in the classrooms
let drivers use loud hydraulic horns
move band practice next to the road
questions.explanation: Signs reduce horn use, and trees and walls block or absorb sound. Soft curtains absorb sound inside the classroom. Loud horns and extra noise make the problem worse.

questions.title: Sound
questions.stem: In the simulation, when you increase the frequency, the waves are drawn closer together and the sound has a higher pitch.

sim.task: Open Sound Waves and choose the Single Source screen. Turn the sound on so that you can hear the speaker. Move the frequency slider from low to high and listen. Watch how close together the waves are.

questions.explanation: A higher frequency means more vibrations each second. The waves are closer together and the pitch is higher.

questions.title: Sound
questions.stem: What happens to the sound when you increase the amplitude and keep the frequency the same?

sim.task: Open Sound Waves and choose the Single Source screen. Turn the sound on. Keep the frequency slider where it is. Move the amplitude slider from low to high, and listen and watch the waves.

options: It gets louder and the pitch goes up.
It gets quieter; the pitch stays the same.
It gets louder; the pitch stays the same.
It gets louder and the pitch goes down.
questions.explanation: Amplitude is the size of the vibrations. Bigger vibrations make a louder sound with taller waves. Pitch depends only on frequency, so it does not change.

questions.title: Sound
questions.stem: What happens to the sound as the air is taken out of the box around the speaker?

sim.task: Open Sound Waves and choose the Air Pressure screen. Turn the sound on and listen. Then use the pump to take the air out of the box around the speaker, and listen again.

options: It gets louder, because the speaker has more space to move in.
It gets quieter, because fewer particles pass on the vibrations.
It stays the same, because the speaker keeps vibrating just as much.
It gets higher in pitch, because there is less air.
questions.explanation: Sound needs particles to pass the vibrations along. With less air there are fewer particles, so less sound reaches your ear. In a vacuum there would be no sound at all.

questions.title: Sound
questions.stem: In the simulation, on both the Water screen and the Sound screen, a bigger amplitude makes taller waves.

sim.task: Open Waves Intro. On the Water screen, move the amplitude slider up and watch the waves. Then choose the Sound screen, turn the sound on, and move the amplitude slider up again.

questions.explanation: Amplitude is the size of the wave. A bigger amplitude gives taller water waves and a louder sound. Waves on different screens follow the same rule.

questions.title: Sound
questions.stem: You hear thunder 3 seconds after you see the lightning. Sound travels about 340 metres each second in air, so the storm is about ___ metres away.
questions.explanation: Light reaches you almost at once, so the 3 seconds is the time taken by the sound. Distance = 340 m/s × 3 s = 1020 m, which is just over 1 km.

questions.title: Sound
questions.stem: Tania twanged a ruler over the edge of a table and a sound app measured the frequency (example results). With 10 cm over the edge it was 120 Hz, 15 cm gave 55 Hz, 20 cm gave 30 Hz and 25 cm gave 20 Hz. What is the best prediction for 12 cm?
options: about 90 Hz
about 40 Hz
about 20 Hz
about 130 Hz
questions.explanation: The frequency falls as more ruler sticks out. 12 cm lies between 10 cm (120 Hz) and 15 cm (55 Hz), so the frequency must lie between 55 and 120 Hz. About 90 Hz fits.

questions.title: Sound
questions.stem: A class measured the loudness at four places with a sound meter app (example readings): school library 35 dB, classroom 60 dB, busy road outside school 85 dB, bus horn nearby 110 dB. A silent zone near a school can have a limit as low as 50 dB in the daytime. Which places are louder than this limit? Choose all that are right.
options: school library
classroom
busy road outside school
bus horn nearby
questions.explanation: Only the library (35 dB) is below 50 dB. The classroom (60), busy road (85) and bus horn (110) are all above it. The road and the horn are also loud enough to harm hearing over time.

questions.title: Sound
questions.stem: Explain why a very loud horn can harm the ear. Use what you know about the eardrum.
questions.model_answer: A very loud sound makes very big vibrations. These make the eardrum and the tiny parts of the cochlea vibrate very strongly, which can damage them and cause hearing loss.
questions.explanation: Loudness depends on the size of the vibrations. Very large vibrations can damage the eardrum and the delicate cochlea, and the damage can be permanent.

questions.title: Sound
questions.stem: A boy taps a long steel rail. His sister at the far end hears two taps: one through the rail and one through the air. Which tap does she hear first, and why?
options: They arrive together, because they come from the same tap.
The tap through the air, because air is lighter and easier to move.
The tap through the rail, because steel carries vibrations faster.
The tap through the air, because it is louder.
questions.explanation: Sound travels at about 5900 metres per second in steel but only 340 in air. The vibrations in the steel get to her ear first, and the sound through the air arrives later.
